metadata.title: David Crowley Defeats Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong in Wisconsin Gubernatorial Primary

sources.news_title: What Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong’s Loss in Wisconsin Really Means for the Democratic Party
sources.text:
This story is adapted from the Slatest newsletter. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every day.
Another Democratic primary, another progressive outsider vs. establishment-backed moderate that ended in a photo finish. Except this time the more moderate candidate won. That’s the story of last night’s highest-profile race, in which David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, narrowly beat Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, to become the party’s nominee for Wisconsin governor. Crowley’s win was also a surprise, making it the second recent primary in which a Midwestern moderate has defied the polls. (In Michigan last week, a centrist congresswoman came from behind and nearly upset Abdul El-Sayed, a Bernie Sanders–endorsed progressive.)
But two elections does not necessarily a pattern make, particularly when those elections yielded two very different winners. And elsewhere, progressives had some big wins in last night’s primaries, so the struggle for the Democratic Party’s future remains far from settled. Let’s get into what happened, what it means, and what it doesn’t mean.
Back up. Who are Crowley and Hong?
Crowley is a former member of the State Assembly who in 2020 became the first Black person to lead Milwaukee County. But after launching his gubernatorial campaign last year, he struggled to gain traction and actually suspended his bid in July. Other moderates also floundered, leaving Hong, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who represents a deep-blue State Assembly district, as the prohibitive favorite. But left-wing comments she made on social media a few years ago put her on the defensive—including support for abolishing the police and canceling Thanksgiving, positions she ultimately disavowed (though, according to my colleague Luke Winkie, not particularly well). Then, in the race’s final weeks, two other moderates dropped out and Crowley revived his campaign with the sitting Democratic governor’s endorsement. He was ultimately the only plausible option for voters worried that Hong’s controversies risked blowing the general election and ended up eking it out by less than half a percentage point.
That’s a tight margin! What else makes his win notable?
Mostly how unexpected it was. As polling booths closed, Hong was overwhelmingly favored on betting markets like Polymarket and Kalshi. That impression was based largely on polls, which showed her roughly doubling Crowley’s support. But in retrospect, it’s probably better to think of the result as a product of very specific circumstances: a field that was fractured among multiple moderates and progressives, Crowley’s late-stage resurrection, a perceived front-runner who was sui generis in the controversies she created, and voters who decided late in the game that Hong risked losing to a Republican in November.
In fairness, Hong barely lost the primary. Why did voters see Crowley but not her as electable?
Electability can be a frustratingly amorphous concept—one that isn’t always fair either. Some voters view female candidates as innately less electable even though political science research suggests that they tend to perform as well as or better than men. On a different note, since Donald Trump’s reelection, many progressives have argued that it’s the Democratic establishment that has lost the capacity—or maybe the right—to discern who is electable. But the evidence also suggests that candidates whom voters perceive as less extreme have a better track record in purple, closely divided states, like … Wisconsin. As mild-mannered Democratic Gov. Tony Evers put it after winning reelection in 2022, “Boring wins.” Hong’s DSA label and progressive platform excited many younger and more educated Wisconsinites, but these qualities evidently raised concerns about her viability statewide for plenty of other Democrats. One of them was Evers, who warned that Hong would “probably” lose to Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee. Notably, many Wisconsin Republicans agreed: GOP-aligned super PACs spent millions to boost Hong’s candidacy, and polls suggested that she would struggle against Tiffany.
Is Hong’s defeat a setback for the left?
It depends who you ask! Some progressives are actually relieved. If Hong had gone on to lose in November, it could’ve become an albatross for their whole movement—and would’ve handed leadership of a swing state to a Trump-endorsed Republican. Even some fellow progressives seemed skeptical of Hong’s campaign and rhetoric; both Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez declined to endorse her. (They claim to be focused on congressional races, but both have endorsed candidates in other kinds of elections too.)
Progressives also have more-straightforward reasons to celebrate: The more-liberal candidates won primaries last night for Vermont governor and for open U.S. Senate and House seats in Minnesota.
So was Crowley’s win the only real bright spot for the Democratic establishment?
No, which is another reason the party’s civil war will almost certainly drag on. Gov. Ned Lamont of Connecticut easily beat back a lefty challenger, moderate Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar romped in her state’s gubernatorial primary, and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the party’s Senate nominee, also in Minnesota. But Flanagan is a progressive as well, a reminder that the establishment–outsider dynamic doesn’t always map perfectly onto the party’s ideological divides.
Another race that exemplifies the varying dynamics at play here: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut, a 78-year-old who suffered a complex partial seizure on the House floor last year, lost his bid for a 15th (!) term to Luke Bronin, a former mayor of Hartford. Larson, a progressive, had support from more-moderate Democrats in Congress, while Bronin, a 47-year-old Navy veteran, ran mostly on generational change with the backing of the Connecticut Democratic Party.
One last question: Given how off the polls were in Wisconsin, should we doubt them going forward?
It’s hard to say! In fairness, getting a bead on a primary in which the candidates keep shifting and many voters remain undecided isn’t easy. Pollsters basically nailed Hong’s share of the vote: Averaged out, surveys over the past month showed her at about 41 percent; she ended up with 39 percent. What the polls generally failed to foresee—and arguably shouldn’t have been expected to, given the fluctuating field—was that just enough voters would ultimately coalesce behind Crowley to put him over the top.
In the aggregate, despite the framing of Crowley’s win as an upset (and it was!), primary polls in other races have tended to be relatively accurate. So although it’s always worth taking them with a grain of salt, last night’s bigger loser was betting markets, whose predictive power in Wisconsin was effectively zero. The ultimate takeaway of all of this might be: If you think you know which faction of the Democratic Party will end up ahead, I have a Polymarket share to sell you. In other words, we’re still in a contentious primary season, and the upshot for the Democrats isn’t clear yet.
OK, I’ve officially maxed out on electoral shop talk for today. To help you avert your gaze from Dems’ slow-rolling identity crisis, my colleagues suggest:
A review of Trump’s “patriotic” art exhibition (yes, that’s a thing): Christina Cauterucci paid a visit to Passport to Patriotism, which functions as the Trump administration’s rebuttal to the Smithsonian’s nuanced interpretation of American history. At the show, Christina found a sea of glittery paintings, several A.I.-augmented portraits of the Founding Fathers, and more than five dozen takes on the American flag. Her dispatch offers an insightful, hilarious window into the MAGA aesthetic.
An eccentric election tradition: If you need a break from U.S. politics, take a peek at what’s happening across the pond. Imogen West-Knights explains the long British tradition of joke candidates and introduces us to Count Binface, an “independent space warrior” who is currently running to unseat Nigel Farage from Parliament.
A defense of Mr. Darcy: Speaking of delightful things the United Kingdom has given us: This analysis of the many discourse cycles that the flawed yet beloved Pride and Prejudice character has set off over the years is a fun one to revisit from Slate’s archives.
A bite-size crossword: Do you ever feel overwhelmed by a full-size crossword puzzle? Do you ever wish for a quick and satisfying little mini one? We have good news for you!
And with that, go enjoy your night! I’ll see you back here tomorrow.

sources.news_title: A surprising comeback in Wisconsin is a reprieve for Democratic moderates
Lindell, Hong suffer primary losses in Minnesota and Wisconsin | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Lindell, Hong suffer primary losses in Minnesota and Wisconsin
Moderate David Crowley beat Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in a tight race for Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary election, a closely watched vote seen as a key test for the appeal of progressive candidates in the battleground state.
According to projections from U.S. media including the Associated Press and NBC News, Milwaukee County Executive Crowley was chosen by Wisconsin Democrats over Hong, who sought to become the state’s first democratic socialist governor.
The nominee will face the Republican’s pick, U.S. Representative Tom Tiffany, in the November general election.
The evening’s primary results in the Upper Midwest also raised questions about the power of an endorsement by U.S. President Donald Trump.
In Minnesota, former MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell lost the Republican nomination for governor to Speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives Lisa Demuth, despite the vocal backing of Trump.
Lindell is an enduring Trump ally and proponent of the false idea that the 2020 presidential election was stolen.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Lindell received Trump’s endorsement in May, when the president wrote on Truth Social, “Mike will be SPECTACULAR!!! He truly loves Minnesota, as do I, and wants to bring it back from oblivion and embarrassment. He can do it!”
Demuth is expected to face a difficult battle with Democratic nominee, Senator Amy Klobuchar, who won her party’s nomination handily, in the aftermath of “Operation Metro Surge,” the immigration deportation campaign in Minneapolis that led to the deaths of two people.
Minnesota’s Democratic Senate primary indicated there is still momentum behind left-leaning candidates, with progressive Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan, who was elected on a ticket with Governor Tim Walz in 2018, beating more moderate Representative Angie Craig.
The candidates are seeking the seat left open by Senator Tina Smith, a Minnesota Democrat who announced her retirement in February 2025. Craig was the only Minnesota Democrat to vote for the Laken Riley Act, which gave the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency broader authority to detain immigrants charged with some crimes, but later said she regretted her vote.
Flanagan has said ICE is out of control and must be dismantled. In Wisconsin, Hong’s left-leaning policy goals, including abolishing ICE, a one-year moratorium on data centers and increased taxation of billionaires and corporations, may be growing in popularity among Democratic voters. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Democratic voters want their party’s candidates to track further to the left. More than seven in 10 liberal Democrats say it’s “essential” for their party’s candidates to support increasing taxes on corporations and billionaires (76%), expanding access to abortion (72%) and universal government-provided healthcare (71%). But unlike Abdul El-Sayed, another progressive who captured the Michigan Democratic Senate primary earlier this month, Hong is running without endorsements from U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
And Hong has faced criticism for the reappearance of old tweets, including a November 2020 post, at the height of a COVID-19 wave, in which she wrote, “Please DON’T gather for the colonizer holiday,” and another when she said, “Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621.”
In recent interviews, Hong has walked back those statements, saying that as a chef, she had fond memories of the Thanksgiving holiday, but that Thanksgiving is a time that is painful for many people. In another interview she said that she did not want to cancel Thanksgiving.
Hong did not respond to a request for an interview. Meanwhile, in Wisconsin’s 3rd congressional district, Democrats chose Rebecca Cooke, a former small business owner and waitress who has run for the seat twice before, as their challenger to Trump-aligned Republican Derrick Van Orden, who has held the district since 2022, in one of the most competitive House races in the country.
Cooke has out-fundraised Van Orden, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has added her to its Red to Blue program, providing organizational and financial support to candidates in the elections it considers the most hotly contested.

sources.news_title: In another key primary test, a favored progressive is upset in Wisconsin governor's race
sources.text:
In another key primary test, a favored progressive is upset in Wisconsin governor’s race
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- David Crowley edged Francesca Hong by just 3,000 votes. He could become Wisconsin’s first Black governor.
- Progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan will face former TV sports reporter Michele Tafoya in the Minnesota Senate race.
WASHINGTON — In another major test of how far left Democratic voters in swing states are willing to go, moderate David Crowley narrowly defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong to become the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin.
The surprise result in Tuesday’s primary — in a closely watched swing state seen as a possible bellwether of Democratic sentiment — came after polls had shown Hong leading the field by double digits. With 95% of the vote counted, Crowley clinched the nomination early Wednesday by just 3,000 votes.
It was the second purple-state race between Democrats in two weeks to have an extremely narrow result, following the slim win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary last week. Polling also overestimated progressive performance in that race.
In the November general election, Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who was endorsed by President Trump. If Crowley were to defeat Tiffany, he would become the first Black governor in the state’s history.
The race had been closely watched as an example of the national fissure between progressive and establishment Democrats.
El-Sayed’s victory will put to the test in a swing state the broader strength of the progressive movement, which has found success in deep-blue places like New York City and Los Angeles.
“Hong’s candidacy is a sign of the broader trends in the party, with outspoken progressives and socialists emerging in some primaries and having real sway in the party,” said University of Wisconsin-Madison professor Barry Burden. “With Crowley, he has a more conciliatory approach ... that probably sits better with the average independent voter or moderate in the state who’s just looking to get some problems addressed.”
Crowley and his backers had undertaken an intense late-July sprint to persuade Democrats to coalesce around him. He suspended his campaign amid low poll numbers, then rejoined the race with less than a month before election day after establishment frontrunner Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out.
“It was fast and furious very late in the campaign to try to build a movement in the party behind Crowley as the establishment candidate who is presumably more likely to win in a general election,” Burden said.
In another upper Midwest contest highlighting the choices confronting Democratic voters, progressive Lt. Gov. Penny Flanagan defeated center-left Rep. Angie Craig. Flanagan will face former television sports reporter Michele Tofoya, a Republican, in November for the seat held by Democratic Sen. Tina Smith, who is retiring.
As Democrats grapple with creating a party identity that will draw swing voters away from President Trump’s Republican Party in November and in 2028, a fierce debate has taken hold between the party’s factions — progressives who argue their approach is the key to the party’s fresh path forward, and moderates who fear that a far-left presidential candidate could cost Democrats the presidency in 2028.
Progressive candidates so far have fared well in blue strongholds such as Denver, New York and Minnesota this cycle, but they have struggled in Missouri and Wisconsin.
“Democrats of all ilk are winning elections all across the country,” said strategist Hyma Moore on Wednesday on CBS News, “and it’s very specific to what that state or that district needs.”
Moore said Hong’s loss was not “a setback for progressives,” arguing that she was a weaker political candidate than Crowley regardless of her ideology.
In his victory remarks Wednesday morning, Crowley rejected the framing of an intra-party conflict.
“We may not agree on every policy, we may not use the same labels, but we all want safe communities, strong schools, affordable healthcare, good-paying jobs and a brighter future for all of our children,” Crowley said.
Hong, a member of the state Assembly, ran into controversy late in the campaign with resurfaced social media posts in which she called for defunding the police and shared her negative opinions on Thanksgiving. Although she sought to retract or revise many of those comments in televised interviews, moderates and centrists seized on these points to argue against her electability.
“She had a whole smorgasbord of positions that were perfectly designed to repel voters in the middle that Democrats have to win,” said Kate deGruyter of the centrist Democratic group Third Way, which is funneling money into an effort to discredit democratic socialism ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Progressive candidates for governor in Wisconsin and U.S. Senate in Minnesota are making their final pushes ahead of Tuesday’s election
The race remained exceedingly tight until early Wednesday, when the Associated Press projected Crowley as the winner. In counties where Crowley was expected to dominate, such as Milwaukee, Hong performed better than expected. While Hong won the city of Madison and areas with University of Wisconsin satellite campuses. the margin was too small to push her past Crowley, according to AP election data.
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) chose to publicly back Hong, but she was unable to secure key national endorsements from the two most prominent progressives in Congress, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).
Hong told her supporters Tuesday night, hours before she conceded, that regardless of the result, progressive politics would have to be reckoned with in Wisconsin’s electoral future.
“We have built something that will change politics forever,” she said. “I am so deeply grateful, to my core, for how hard you have all fought, and for what this fight, our movement, means for all of Wisconsin.”
Times staff writer Justine McDaniel in Washington contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Far-Left, Anti-Israel Candidate Falls Short in Wisconsin Democratic Governor’s Primary
sources.text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong takes to the stage at her primary election watch party at Atwood Music Hall Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, in Madison. Photo: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
In a stunning upset, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly defeated democratic socialist state Rep. Francesca Hong in Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary early Wednesday morning, dealing a setback to the party’s progressive wing in one of the most closely contested political battlegrounds in the United States.
Crowley’s victory came in a dramatic political comeback after Hong had emerged as a leading progressive contender and held a double-digit edge in polling in the closing weeks of the campaign.
Crowley ultimately prevailed by just over 3,000 votes, winning approximately 39.8 percent to Hong’s 39.4 percent, according to results reported after Tuesday’s primary.
The result positions Crowley, a more centrist Democrat, to face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November in a race that could determine the political direction of Wisconsin, a pivotal Midwestern swing state.
The primary represented a closely watched test of the Democratic Party’s ideological trajectory. Hong campaigned as a democratic socialist and progressive outsider, adopting unorthodox policy positions on an array of economic and cultural issues. Hong’s membership in the politically ascendant and anti-Israel group the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) drew heightened scrutiny in the weeks leading up to the election.
In a variety of interviews, Hong accused Israel of committing a “genocide” in Gaza and also promised to repeal the International Holocaust Remembrance Association (IHRA) definition of antisemitism from state law if elected governor.
“Protest is free speech and direct democracy. And right now, we have an anti-BDS [boycott, divestment, and sanctions] law on the books that we’ve had legislation we’ve introduced to repeal, so that the state is not interfering in the right to protest,” she said in an interview with Vox Magazine.
“We have passed the IHRA definition of antisemitism: the IHRA legislation, here in our state, that was quite controversial. I would be looking at potentially repealing that legislation,” she added.
An intergovernmental organization comprising dozens of countries, IHRA adopted the “working definition” of antisemitism in 2016. Since then, the definition has gained widespread support from Jewish organizations and lawmakers around the world, and is now used by hundreds of governmental bodies, including the European Union and the United Nations. However, critics argue that it infringes on free speech by including Holocaust denial and modern forms targeting Israel, such as demonizing the Jewish state and denying its right to exist.
Hong’s anti-Israel posture earned her an endorsement from the Wisconsin Muslim Civic Alliance (WMCA), citing her “positions on the IHRA definition and Wisconsin’s anti-BDS law.”
“Fran has consistently stood with us on principle, by opposing the IHRA definition, introducing legislation to oppose Wisconsin’s anti-BDS law, and supporting our efforts even when it was not politically convenient,” WMCA wrote in a statement.
Leaders of the BDS movement, which seeks to isolate Israel on the international stage, have repeatedly stated their goal is to destroy the world’s only Jewish state.
Hong also sparked outrage when she co-hosted a campaign fundraising event alongside antisemitic streamer Michael Beyer, who goes by the name “MikeFromPA” online. Beyer has called Jews a “constructed” and “demonic” ethnic group. He has also stated that he aims to expel “Zionists” from the Democratic Party entirely.
The state lawmaker further drew criticism for appearing on the livestream of anti-Israel social media pundit Hasan Piker in June. Piker has a long record of inflammatory rhetoric concerning Israel, Jews, and terrorism. He has expressed support for Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis; cast doubt on documented evidence of sexual violence during Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, massacre; compared Zionism to Nazism; and referred to Orthodox Jews as “inbred,” a remark for which he later expressed regret.
Brushing aside criticism of her association with Piker, Hong invited him for a campaign rally in the lead-up to Election Day.
Crowley, Hong’s opponent, benefited from support from Wisconsin’s Democratic establishment, including outgoing Gov. Tony Evers. His campaign focused heavily on electability and the argument that Democrats needed a candidate capable of building a broad coalition in a closely divided state. Unlike Hong, Crowley adopted more moderate positions on economic and cultural issues and did not center opposition to Israel in his campaign.
Hong also faced attacks over controversial statements and positions from earlier in her political career, including past comments concerning support for abolishing the police and even canceling Thanksgiving. While she subsequently distanced herself from some of those positions, Republicans and other critics repeatedly used them to portray her as outside the political mainstream.
The Wisconsin result comes as progressive and democratic socialist candidates continue to make gains in parts of the Democratic Party, but those victories have not been nationwide. While progressives scored important wins elsewhere in Tuesday’s primaries, Crowley’s victory demonstrates that Democratic voters in a critical swing state remain receptive to candidates emphasizing moderation and general-election viability.
Crowley, who could become Wisconsin’s first Black governor, will now attempt to consolidate Democratic support before turning his attention to Tiffany, a Republican backed by President Donald Trump.
For the Democratic Party, Crowley’s victory offers a counterpoint to the narrative of an accelerating socialist shift within its ranks. Anti-Israel progressives have enjoyed a string of high-profile victories in Michigan, Colorado, and New York City, oftentimes toppling moderates who adopted a more moderate approach to the Jewish state.
For pro-Israel advocates, Hong’s defeat represents a brief reprieve from opponents of the Jewish state securing victories in high-profile Democratic contests.

sources.news_title: Democratic primary voters pick anti-MAGA candidates for November ballots
sources.text:
The corporate media is making much of the battles between so-called “establishment” Democrats and others who are identified with the organization Democratic Socialists of America. While the divisions are real enough, reliance on such broad categories sometimes cloud the facts.
Similarly, too many commentators seem intent on pitting Black voters against white progressive voters in the Democratic Party, underemphasizing the determination of both to make major changes in November.
Last night, voters selected candidates they see as seriously addressing affordability and the crisis of democracy. In all the primaries, Democratic turnout was huge, outpacing the GOP and portending good results for opponents of MAGA.
A Democratic U.S. Senate primary in Minnesota turned into a progressive rout for Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. An expected win in the gubernatorial primary in next-door Wisconsin for Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong turned into a narrow loss to David Crowley.
Nevertheless, results show that, even with a candidate like Hong losing narrowly to Crowley, Democratic voters are not always happy with so-called establishment politicians. Connecticut voters in the Hartford-based 1st Congressional District, for example, reinforced this point: Incumbent Rep. John Larson, 78, first elected in 1998, lost to his top challenger, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, by a wide margin.
First, the winners in Minnesota:
Flanagan, a progressive who campaigned on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires and millionaires more, and who shunned corporate campaign cash, had slim polling leads over her foe, self-described “moderate” U.S. Rep. Angie Craig. Voters chose Flanagan by 19 percentage points (59% to 40%) and 136,907 votes.
If she wins the fall election to the U.S. Senate against the GOP nominee—former NFL sideline broadcaster Michele Tafoya—Flanagan will be the first-ever Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate.
Flanagan had widespread progressive support, and the foot soldiers for her showed it. Sen. Bernie Sanders, Ind-Vt., supported her but stayed silent about the race in Wisconsin, as did retiring Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) Sen. Tina Smith, whom Flanagan hopes to succeed, and Rep. Ilhan Omar, DFL-Minn., an outspoken foe of President Donald Trump.
“Peggy campaigned on…the idea that one good job should be enough to pay your bills—and she did it without taking corporate PAC money,” the Progressive Change Campaign Committee said in a fundraising letter for her and the rest of its Senate slate.
“She has credibility with voters because she’s already delivered paid family and medical leave, free school meals, lower prescription drug costs, and historic investments in affordable housing,” PCCC said.
In the open 2nd Congressional District, which Craig is vacating, State Sen. Matt Little, DFL-Lakeville, its former mayor and a backer of Medicare for All and foe of corporate financing of elections, easily won the Democratic nomination in a four-way race. He’ll now run for Craig’s open seat, which leans Democratic.
One of his foes, State Rep. Kaela Berg, an Association of Flight Attendants-CWA member who finished third, had to take leave from her full-time job as an airline cabin attendant to campaign. She, too, emphasized progressive stands and accountability.
In the Minneapolis-based 5th Congressional District, Omar got endorsements from both the Minneapolis and St. Paul Regional Labor Federations and easily won. She’s expected to romp in the fall.
State Attorney General Keith Ellison, a leader among Attorneys General nationwide in opposing Trump’s racism, won 85% to 15%. After months of legal wrestling with Trump’s ICE troops, Ellison and his staff finally won access to the federal evidence—which may now be legally “contaminated”—from their killings of peaceful protest observers Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, an RN and American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) member.
Including outside spending, Craig outspent Flanagan by an enormous margin. But in a state where 94% of Democrats oppose Trump and his fatal “Operation Metro Surge” in the Twin Cities, Craig’s support for prior Trump/GOP legislation to turn ICE loose and the Laken Riley Act hurt her. The rest of the state’s Democrats opposed ICE and that law, too.
Flanagan’s stand against ICE and its sweep energized many Twin Cities voters. Andrea Gaitan, a St. Paul voter, exclaimed “Peggy!” when the St. Paul Pioneer Press asked who she voted for. Gaitan explained Craig’s stand on ICE had “pissed her off.” Susan Landis of the suburb of Cottage Grove said Craig’s shifts showed her the congresswoman didn’t really know what she stands for.
Even Minnesota Republicans got into the upset act on Aug. 11, in their gubernatorial primary. They turned away from Trump extremist, election conspiracy spouter Mike Lindell, who had the president’s backing and—as CEO of MyPillow—plenty of corporate campaign cash.
Moderate-conservative Lisa Demuth, the state House Speaker, won that three-way race with 43% of the vote. She’ll face the state’s other DFL U.S. senator, Amy Klobuchar, for the right to enter the governor’s mansion. Incumbent DFL Gov. Tim Walz, a union teacher scarred by scandals in state aid, is retiring.
Unlike Lindell, Demuth does not believe in outsourcing the jobs of 40% of the state’s workers, abolishing most aid to education, and eliminating the state income tax in favor of sales taxes, which fall most heavily on poor and middle-income people, while barely bothering the 1%.
Back in Wisconsin, the usual rule if you’re a progressive and you want to win the Democratic Party primary, sweep the college towns. But as Hong learned on primary day, you need a little bit more than that.
Hong, who is a state representative, part-time bartender, single mother, and DSA member, accomplished the collegiate sweep in her gubernatorial race against Crowley, the Milwaukee County Executive, but it wasn’t enough.
Hong beat Crowley in Dane County, home of the University of Wisconsin’s 30,000-plus student main campus in Madison, by approximately 10,000 votes. She lost Crowley’s home Milwaukee County—which includes the city and a University of Wisconsin commuter campus—by 2,400.
Everywhere else there was a big college in Wisconsin—Green Bay and its suburbs, Appleton, Eau Claire in the west, Racine in the southeast, Menominee County in the northeast, and so on—Hong won.
With 95%+ of the vote counted, however, Crowley had a 3,885-vote lead (39.9% to 39.4%) out of 783,112 ballots cast. State Sen. Kelda Roys, the former director of Wisconsin Planned Parenthood, took 58,610 votes (7.5%). The New York Times election team said Roys may have siphoned vital votes from Hong in Dane County (Madison), which Hong represents in the statehouse. Roys got 16,100 votes there.
Hong favored fully funding the state share of school spending. She campaigned against taxpayer-paid vouchers for parents of private school kids. She said she wants to limit the impact of artificial intelligence in hiring and firing workers and ban data centers. She backed universal child care.
Hong picked up endorsements from young city, town, and county leaders and state legislators, from a Teachers/AFT local, from the Progressive Democrats of America and Our Revolution, and from the Service Employees.
Crowley ran on electability, pointing out he had carried Milwaukee County, the state’s most-populous, three times. He had significant labor backing, securing the support of the Professional Firefighters, the Wisconsin Laborers’ District Council, the state Electrical Workers council, the Midwest regional body of the Carpenters, and locals of the Operating Engineers and Plumbers unions.
Gov. Tony Evers, U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore, and dozens of state lawmakers, mayors, and other officials also gave him their endorsements.
His platform focuses on reforming the tax system rather than the more significant overhaul proposed by Hong, tighter regulation of data centers (but not an outright ban on their construction), more funding for special education, and expanding the public healthcare program.
Crowley is expected, if he wins the governorship in November, to continue his policy of opposing the Trump agenda. He will face U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump backer and vice-chair of the far-right House Freedom Caucus. Tiffany beat an unknown foe, taking 95% of the GOP primary vote.

sources.news_title: What Francesca Hong’s Defeat Means for Democrats
sources.text:
Outside of Presidential elections, most political races—even those on which the future of a party is said to hinge—are fiercely contested by only a small number of people. Last night, in Madison, Wisconsin, I pulled up a little late to what was supposed to be a victory party for Francesca Hong, a democratic-socialist state legislator whose rise in the state’s gubernatorial primary was understood to portend a major breakthrough for the left. There was no trouble getting inside. A music venue had been rented for a crowd of around seven hundred people, and the event had the scale, and the feel, of a punk show in a college town. An activist I was talking with sounded a little amazed that there were so many reporters in the press section. Then, as the results came in, the crowd thinned.
That Hong’s candidacy was treated as a big political-news event reflected the momentum generated by left-wing candidates this year, and the electoral risks that they are sometimes said to pose for the Democratic Party. The left had built on Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York’s mayoral race, with victories by democratic socialists over incumbents in a few congressional primaries this summer, in districts in New York City and Denver. The question this month was whether the left could also win statewide primaries in less progressive states, and polls showed both Abdul El-Sayed, running for the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, and Hong winning handily. Last Tuesday, El-Sayed, who is not a democratic socialist but who had campaigned with Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Elizabeth Warren, narrowly won his primary. Yesterday, Hong, who is a democratic socialist but had none of those endorsements, narrowly lost her race to David Crowley, the Milwaukee County Executive.
The final days of the Wisconsin contest were dominated by the presence of Tony Evers, the sitting governor who declined to seek another term. He travelled the state, saying loudly and a little grouchily that Democrats were on the verge of a huge mistake and that their voters needed to get their acts together. (To be fair to the voters, the Party’s elected officials had struggled to get their own act together; Crowley had initially dropped out of the race, after drawing little support, only to reënter as two other candidates who had been running well ahead of him—Sara Rodriguez and Mandela Barnes—dropped out.) Evers, a seventy-four-year-old former science teacher, is not normally the loudest or most confrontational of politicians, so his forcefulness got attention. When a reporter with the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel asked Evers whether Hong, then seen as the front-runner, would be able to beat the Republican Tom Tiffany, a pro-Trump congressman, in the general election, the governor eschewed partisan protocol and said, “Probably not.”
Was Hong, who lost to Crowley by a few thousand votes, unelectable? She had an interesting mix of strengths and weaknesses that made her a little different from a generic left-wing candidate. Raised in Madison by Korean-immigrant parents, she had dropped out of the University of Wisconsin and worked her way up in restaurants, from a dishwasher to the owner of a ramen shop, before running for the state legislature on a progressive platform supporting expanded unionization and a more skeptical view of the police. Early in the gubernatorial campaign, Hong had proposed a moratorium on data centers in the state, a politically perceptive choice that took advantage of public antipathy toward Silicon Valley billionaires and which reached far beyond her left-wing audience. (Politicians from the centrist Democratic governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, to the very conservative governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, have since taken up the anti-data-center banner.) But, unlike Mamdani, or El-Sayed, Hong wasn’t a natural on broadcast media, and, when reporters raised what seemed like performative old tweets of hers (she had denounced both Thanksgiving and fireworks), she could not straightforwardly explain or dismiss them. Instead, she wound up in the reduced and defensive position of insisting to Politico that, in fact, she loved Thanksgiving.
That the upper echelon of the Democratic Party’s left wing mostly stayed away from this race makes Hong’s defeat a little less significant; it also shows some savvy on the part of Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders. And the remarkably strong turnout of Democratic voters across these primaries is a very good sign for the Party’s prospects in November. Even so, the final stages of the race in Wisconsin this week offered some clarity about why neither part of the Democratic Party has yet been able to decisively beat the other.
For all its avowals of awakening a broad working-class movement, the left remains mostly the faction of the young, educated, urban middle class, and its candidates have struggled among older, non-college-educated, and suburban and rural voters, both in races that they’ve won, such as in Michigan, and lost, as in Wisconsin. El-Sayed, a more obviously talented political performer than Hong, faced a minor scandal of his own this week, when CNN reported that he had made private more than a hundred YouTube videos he’d recorded between 2022 and 2024, which included some lightly embarrassing progressive posturing, notably an opposition to fireworks. On ABC’s “This Week,” Ocasio-Cortez tried to excuse such statements as part of the social experience of the pandemic: “Woke 1 was crazy.” But the candidates she was defending were mature politicians when they made those comments—El-Sayed, a Rhodes Scholar and former Wayne County health director, had already run for statewide office—who, in general elections, will need to find a more convincing explanation for why they no longer believe in the bold-sounding remarks they made a short time ago.
The trouble for the rest of the Democratic Party is about newness. There are still only three sitting democratic-socialist members of Congress. That this tiny faction has been the major story of the midterm elections shows how much difficulty the rest of the Party has had in making a compelling case. Hong’s early capture of the data-center issue, which was not especially ideological, is a good example of how consistently the Party’s much larger traditional wing has been out-hustled. When I watched debates between left-wing and established candidates this spring, and heard the incumbents rattling off their accomplishments, I often thought, That’s it? (Anyone denouncing the upset victory of the democratic-socialist activist Darializa Avila Chevalier over Representative Adriano Espaillat in a northern Manhattan and Bronx congressional primary, for instance, should take in the meek case that Espaillat made for himself in their debate.) A decade into the Trump era, for incumbents to ask for voters’ support by promising that they are “fighters” and criticizing the right-wing agenda, as many did this cycle, won’t cut it. When CNN sent its feed to Wisconsin, even as the results went against the left, the cameras turned, again and again, to Hong’s “victory” party. Crowley, the winner of the primary and probably the slight favorite to be elected governor, was barely in the picture.
It is strange to go through a period of such apparent tumult in the Party and see a stubborn, unresolved status quo. And yet, as the primary season ends, that is the basic situation. In the half century since the civil-rights movement, a period whose main patterns have been the progress of cultural liberalism and the politics of conservative backlash, the Democratic Party has largely been shaped by two defining figures: Bill Clinton and Barack Obama. It still awaits a third. For all the interest and momentum that the left has generated this year, it is still probably the smaller faction. But those who stand outside of it—call them centrists, liberals, or traditional progressives—are undoubtedly the duller ones. In Milwaukee this morning, the summer haze was thick, the public biergartens in the parks were awaiting the post-work crowds, and most of Wisconsin’s population was left with the quizzical aftermath of a remarkably heated and only partly resolved argument that was contested by about an eighth of them. ♦

sources.news_title: David Crowley Defeats Francesca Hong in Wisconsin Governor Democratic Primary
Republican election meddling has crashed into a brick wall: analysis
sources.text:
The Republican Party's attempt to manipulate Democratic primaries by boosting beatable candidates is falling flat on its face.
According to MS NOW's Steve Benen, the loss by progressive Francesca Hong on Tuesday night in Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, despite Republican PACs spending millions on ads supporting her, showed voters have caught on to the "meddling."
As he wrote, Republicans had identified Rep. Tom Tiffany, an election denier and member of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, as their likely nominee. Recognizing that Tiffany would struggle in a statewide race in one of the country's "most competitive battlegrounds," the party decided to intervene in the Democratic primary.
The strategy was straightforward: spend millions of dollars to support Francesca Hong, a Democratic Socialist state lawmaker, turning the race into a referendum on her progressive views and controversial social media history to alienate moderate voters and independents and take the focus off Tiffany's MAGA ties.
According to Benen, "Following Hong’s narrow loss, the party’s win-loss record can charitably be described as a mixed bag. The fine folks at The Downballot have kept a running list of 2026 races in which Republicans have tried to boost a specific Democratic candidate in the primary, and with primary season nearly over, the GOP has racked up more failures than successes."
The party's record shows only five successful examples of GOP meddling compared to 11 failures, the report notes, with Benen writing, "The plan had a certain logic to it, but it didn’t work out."

sources.news_title: David Crowley defeats Francesca Hong in Wisconsin Governor Democratic primary - The Tribune
sources.text:
Wisconsin [US], August 12 (ANI): David Crowley, the top elected official in Milwaukee County, defeated state representative and democratic socialist Francesca Hong in Tuesday's (local time) Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor, according to The Washington Post.
Crowley, 40, will face Republican nominee Tom Tiffany, a congressman from Wisconsin's rural north, in the November general election. Tiffany, 68, defeated political newcomer Andy Manske in the Republican primary.
Socialist Francesca Hong had led Crowley in several polls by wide margins ahead of the election. However, she faced scrutiny in the final stages of the campaign over her past calls to abolish the police and cancel Thanksgiving, positions that some Democrats feared could hurt her chances in the November election, as reported by the Washington Post.
According to the report, Crowley's victory gives the Democratic Party establishment a win over its progressive wing. He campaigned as a pragmatist and received the backing of a retiring Democratic Governor Tony Evers.
Crowley served in the Wisconsin state legislature for three years before being elected Milwaukee County executive in 2020. Milwaukee is the state's most populous county.
Tiffany has represented Wisconsin in the US House since winning a special election in 2020. Before entering Congress, he spent a decade in the state legislature.
Crowley and Tiffany will now face each other in the November 2026 general election for Wisconsin governor.
Throughout the whole day, US state primary elections delivered major victories and crushing defeats, with Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth handing Trump-backed Mike Lindell a primary loss in the Republican governor's race, while in South Carolina, appointed Senator Darline Graham and Representative Ralph Norman beat out candidates to advance to a runoff for the state's vacant US Senate seat.
In a notable setback for US President Donald Trump's primary endorsement record, MyPillow founder Mike Lindell was defeated in Minnesota's Republican gubernatorial primary by state House Speaker Lisa Demuth, according to CNN.
The result came despite Trump issuing an explicit endorsement hours before polls closed, writing on Truth Social that Lindell "deserves a BIG WIN IN MINNESOTA today."
Demuth prevailed in a raucous, three-way contest against Lindell and Kendall Qualls, an Army veteran and former healthcare executive. According to CNN, while Qualls won the state GOP's endorsement at its convention and Lindell held Trump's endorsement, Demuth prevailed by pressing her legislative accomplishments and experience.
Celebrating her victory, Demuth, in a post on X, said, "It's an absolute honor to be the Republican candidate for governor of Minnesota. Today was a major milestone in this campaign, but we're not done yet. Tonight, Minnesotans made it clear they are ready for real change - at the top. It's time to end the fraud, restore common sense to our state government and return Minnesota to a place that works for families, seniors, businesses and our next generation. Let's go win in November!"
She will advance to face Democratic candidate and current US Sen. Amy Klobuchar in November.
On the Democratic side in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan secured the nomination for the US Senate seat being vacated by outgoing Senator Tina Smith, defeating moderate candidate Rep. Angie Craig.
Flanagan, a progressive who secured the state party's endorsement in May with backing from Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, had criticised her opponent in November, Republican Michele Tafoya, saying that she is a "loyal soldier" to President Donald Trump and does not understand the struggles people are experiencing in their lives, according to CNN.
Following the race, Angie Craig extended her support to Peggy Flanagan, stating in a post on X, "Peggy Flanagan's commitment to Minnesota and dedication to improving the lives of everyone around her is admirable -- I offer her my wholehearted support."
In South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman advanced to an August 25 runoff in the special Republican primary to complete the term of the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Graham thanked President Donald Trump for his "steadfast support and his complete and total endorsement," and retold the story of growing up with her brother in the back of the bar of a liquor store to highlight her work ethic. (ANI)
(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

sources.news_title: A DSA candidate lost a messy race for Wisconsin governor
sources.text:
Following a chaotic race for Wisconsin governor, moderate Democrat David Crowley defeated progressive Francesca Hong on Tuesday night.
Although Hong held a convincing lead in many of Tuesday’s polls, she lost by about 4,000 votes—a narrow 0.5 percentage point. As someone presenting herself as a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and without endorsements from key progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.)—who notably distanced herself from more progressive policies on Sunday, Hong came across as an outsider candidate who gained popularity over time.
Critics on the right, and some Democrats, criticized Hong for past social media remarks, such as a deleted post to “Cancel Thanksgiving” and calls for “defunding the police as a first step towards abolishing the police”. If she won, she would have become the first democratic socialist governor in US history.
On the establishment Democrats’ side, multiple candidates who were once considered front-runners withdrew—including Sara Rodriguez, Wisconsin’s current lieutenant governor, who suspended her campaign in mid-July after she fired her campaign manager for inflating financial reports. Even the victor, Crowley, re-entered the race shortly after Rodriguez’s departure (he initially suspended his campaign in early July due in part to poor polling).
It was a messier race than others where progressives won, such as Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate primary victory in Michigan, and may provide fewer clear takeaways about the future of progressives running as Democrats.

sources.news_title: 'Are You 'Serious?' — NBC Data Guru Stunned After Last-Minute Votes Come In
sources.text:
NBC chief data analyst Steve Kornacki was in absolute disbelief on Tuesday night as a handful of unbelievable election results poured in throughout the night.
Kornacki faced a tough night on Tuesday as some unforeseen twists in the razor-thin Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary unfolded, with former Thanksgiving hater and democratic socialist Francesca Hong (D) losing to David Crowley (D).
Kornacki seemed like he was on the verge of walking off-set and never returning—but it made for some good clips, which were shared on social media.
With 93% of the votes counted and Crowley narrowly leading by about 3,200 votes, it was clear Kornacki was not pleased to hear that.
Kornacki slouched over and put his hands on his knees for a few seconds before mustering the strength to pull himself up again. But his mouth was agape in sheer disbelief.
“Really? Really?” he muttered quietly. “That’s um… so we’re back to square one on this?”
Additionally, Kornacki laughed angrily and buried his head in his left palm when he learned that there would be delays due to Milwaukee County officials’ announcement that five flash drives had corrupted voting data.
“Are you serious?! They have to… God… what were… OK…umm,” Kornacki said as he looked down at his New Balance sneakers in disbelief.
Another clip of Kornacki saying that NBC News was waiting on Wisconsin officials to “get their act together” also went pretty viral.
He looked into the camera and told viewers that he was disappointed that he’d have to sign off without giving them the results many of them had been waiting hours to hear.
“I hate doin’ this to you, because I know you’re here for results,” Kornacki vented.
The results finally trickled in, and Hong conceded early Wednesday morning that she lost to Crowley by several thousand votes.
Not long after, Kornacki yelled out to the NBC News faithful who battled the election madness.
“Thank you *so* much to everyone who joined in for our livestream last night. I couldn’t believe how many of you were right there with me as Milwaukee kept us waiting (and waiting) into the wee hours,” he posted on X. “I hope you got at least a little sleep!”
WATCH:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley secured a narrow upset victory in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor on Tuesday, defeating socialist State Rep. Francesca Hong.
With nearly all votes counted, Crowley captured 39.8 percent (313,321 votes) to Hong’s 39.4 percent (310,109 votes), a margin of roughly 3,200 votes.
State Sen. Kelda Roys finished third with 7.5 percent, followed by former state administration secretary Joel Brennan at 4.7 percent and Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez (who had suspended her campaign) at 4.1 percent.
The Associated Press called the race for Crowley early Wednesday after Hong conceded, eliminating the prospect of a recount in the exceptionally close contest.
The outcome marked a stunning comeback for Crowley, 40, who had suspended his campaign in early July amid lagging support and endorsed Rodriguez.
After Rodriguez exited days later amid a campaign finance scandal, Crowley re-entered the race with the strong backing of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, who recruited him as a moderate alternative.
Evers’ endorsement and late fundraising surge helped Crowley consolidate establishment support in the final weeks.
Hong, a Madison representative and the first Asian American elected to the Wisconsin Legislature, had led public polls by double digits—sometimes as much as 20 to 30 points—and energized progressive voters with a platform focused on workers’ rights, housing, and expanded social programs.
Her campaign sought to build on recent progressive successes elsewhere, but moderate and pragmatic Democratic voters prioritized electability in the swing state.
Crowley, who would become Wisconsin’s first Black governor if elected in November, emphasized affordability, jobs, education, and his personal story of overcoming homelessness as a child.
Crowley will face Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump-backed congressman who easily won his primary, in the November general election.
The open seat becomes available as Evers declines a third term.
The Democratic primary’s razor-thin result highlighted ongoing tensions between the party’s progressive and moderate wings in a critical battleground, with Crowley arguing he is better positioned to hold the governorship.
This article may contain commentary which reflects the author's opinion.

sources.news_title: Israel detains Palestinian journalist Mohamed Awad; Russia threatens retaliatory European ship seizures; Hong loses in tight primary for Wisconsin governor
sources.text:
Israel detains Palestinian journalist Mohamed Awad; Russia threatens retaliatory European ship seizures; Hong loses in tight primary for Wisconsin governor
Drop Site Daily: August 12, 2026
Wednesday, August 12, 2026 – Pakistani Interior Minister arrives in Tehran. Iranian National Security Head pares down Hormuz conditions. U.S. claims 9 million barrels of oil pass through Hormuz daily. Clashes reported in Iraqi Kurdistan. Former Mossad chief alleges spies repeatedly visited Fordow nuclear site. Ansarallah launches new attack on Al-Makha. Death toll from Ansarallah attack on vessel rises to six. U.S. strikes in Yemen killed 153 civilians, Pentagon says. Israel detains Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Mohamed Awad. Conditions for Palestinian prisoners in Israel’s Ganot prison deteriorating rapidly. UN: Thousands in Gaza still await medical evacuation. Israel continues to ravage the occupied West Bank. Security Council holds West Bank meeting, official says area "at breaking point". NCAG meets with UN. Israel continues attacks in Lebanon despite "ceasefire" framework. Lebanon becomes first Arab country to abolish death penalty. Lebanon passes first general amnesty law since 1991. Tuesday's primary results. AP: ICE plans to give agents gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks. Paramount CEO threatens California exit. Hegseth's Pentagon advisory board appointees have financial ties to Trump family-linked venture fund. Justice Samuel Alito made up to $2.9 million from fossil fuel holdings since 2005. Mayor Mamdani vs. Amazon. General Dynamics's $533 million Texas artillery factory never produced a usable shell, investigation finds. Russia threatens to seize European vessels in retaliation for possible ship seizures. 15 killed and dozens missing after ferry capsizes in Zimbabwe. Ten Nigerian police officers killed in clash with bandits in Kebbi state. Colombia and Venezuela rebuild ties with Israel. North Korea launches ballistic missile ahead of U.S.–South Korean military drills. UNESCO says 2.4 million Afghan girls remain barred from secondary education.
TONIGHT: Join our live event on Israel's Lobby.
Authors Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick join Ryan Grim and Murtaza Hussain live at 7PM ET, your questions answered on the spot. Paid subscriber exclusive.
Iran
- Pakistani Interior Minister arrives in Tehran: Pakistan’s interior minister Mohsin Naqvi arrived in Tehran on Wednesday for a meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, part of mediation efforts to halt the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Al Jazeera. 
  - A spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry said after the meeting that Pakistan was “working to bring” the U.S. and Iran “to the negotiating table.”
  - Pakistan, alongside Qatar, has been a principal mediator in the five-month conflict, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
- Iranian National Security Head pares down Hormuz conditions: Mohsen Rezaei, the newly appointed Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, laid out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, saying in a post on X that Iran would not reopen the Strait “until the U.S. ends the war and blockade, releases Iran’s frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Gaza.” 
  - “Until all conditions are met, the strait will remain closed,” he reiterated.
  - The list is narrower than that presented by his predecessor, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, on August 8, which also included full compensation for war damages and sanctions relief, and which explicitly included Yemen and Iraq in its ceasefire call.
- U.S. claims 9 million barrels of oil pass through Hormuz daily: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright claimed on Tuesday that military operations and cooperation with Gulf allies had pushed the seven-day average for oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz to nearly 9 million barrels per day. 
  - In a post on X, he claimed more than 20 million barrels left the region on Sunday alone, exceeding prewar levels, without providing a source for his estimates.
  - Kpler estimated exports of 2.3 million barrels per day last week, and even with “dark transits,” experts still say that the true number falls far short of Wright’s Tuesday estimates.
  - Separately on Wednesday, the International Energy Agency (IEA) projected that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day (bpd), or about 4%, this year, citing disruptions both in Hormuz and the Bab Al-Mandab Straits. The 4.3 million bpd supply drop is larger than the 3.7 million bpd reduction forecast in the IEA’s July report.
- Clashes reported in Iraqi Kurdistan: Iran fired several missiles and drones at locations in Iraq’s Erbil province on Wednesday, a Kurdish Peshmerga commander told Rudaw, targeting fighters from the Komala Party and the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI). No casualties were reported. 
  - Al Jazeera reported that four drones hit Erbil, and cited a separate report from Reuters, which said that the attacks targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition camps in the region.
- IRGC adviser discusses war strategy with U.S. media: In a Tuesday interview with PBS, senior IRGC adviser Mohammad Reza Naqdi said Iran has thwarted Washington’s objectives, learned how to fight the U.S. military, and may prolong the war until the next American presidency to impose sustained costs and establish deterrence. 
  - Naqdi told PBS that Washington failed to topple Iran’s leadership or break the country apart, leaving it to wage “a war without a strategy” and repeatedly announce new objectives.
  - “We have also seen how the American military is weaker than what we perceived,” he said.
  - The adviser said Iran has “no need” for a nuclear weapon, citing popular support for the country during the war.
  - When asked why Iran’s new supreme leader has not appeared publicly during the war, Naqdi claimed it was for security reasons.
- Iran to join BRICS’s New Development Bank: Iran will soon join the BRICS-backed New Development Bank (NDP), Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said Wednesday ahead of a BRICS finance meeting in India, according to Reuters. (BRICS is Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa.) Hemmati said Tehran sees the bank as one of the most important outcomes of BRICS cooperation and is also seeking greater bilateral and trilateral monetary cooperation with member states, including conducting trade in national currencies. 
  - Iran joined BRICS in 2024 and has since sought membership and a shareholding in the NDB, which was established in 2015 to finance infrastructure and sustainable development projects.
- Former Mossad chief alleges spies repeatedly visited Fordow nuclear site: Yossi Cohen, who led Mossad from 2015 to 2021, claimed that Israeli spies “toured” Iran’s Fordow nuclear site “many times” to understand the facility, at a conference on Tuesday. 
  - Cohen did not specify when the visits occurred or who carried them out, and offered no further evidence.
  - He added that the American bombing of Fordow was “the fulfillment of all my dreams,” a reference to U.S. strikes on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan during the 12-day war Washington and Israel launched against Iran in June 2025.
Yemen
- Ansarallah launches new attack on Al-Makha: Ansarallah launched new ballistic missile attacks on the strategic port of Al-Makha (Mocha) near the Bab Al-Mandab Strait in southwestern Yemen, Saba TV reported on Wednesday. 
  - The attack comes one day after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said Ansarallah had launched 10 ballistic missiles and four drones at the city.
- Death toll from Ansarallah attack on vessel rises to six: The death toll from an attack by Ansarallah on a Yemeni commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Tuesday has risen to six people, including three Pakistani nationals. Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar condemned the attack in a post on X. “Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea,” Dar wrote.
- U.S. strikes in Yemen killed 153 civilians, Pentagon says: The Pentagon admitted to Congress in a report on Wednesday that U.S. airstrikes killed 153 civilians and wounded 243 others in Yemen last year. 
  - The deaths come from three April 2025 strikes: one that killed five, another that killed 80, and a third that killed 68. Human Rights Watch had said the second of these, a strike on the Ras Isa fuel port, should be investigated as a war crime.
  - The Yemen Data Project has recorded at least 238 civilians killed and 467 wounded in the campaign, which ran from March to May 2025 and was codenamed Operation Rough Rider, and the monitor Airwars put the toll around 258.
Palestine
- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, two Palestinians were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. One body was also recovered from beneath the rubble. 
  - The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,388 killed, with 174,259 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,259 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,148, while 808 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.
- Israel detains Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Mohamed Awad: Israeli forces detained Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Mohamed Awad, 38, from his home in Bitunia, west of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, early Wednesday morning. Two other Palestinians were arrested after raiding and searching their homes in the nearby city of Al-Bireh, according to Wafa. 
  - Soldiers first raided an apartment in a different neighborhood that Awad’s family had moved out of months earlier, breaking down the door only to find it empty, Awda’s wife Eman Awad told Al-Araby.
  - They then went on foot to the family’s current home and pounded on the door until Awad opened it. He was blindfolded, handcuffed behind his back, and forced to walk down five flights of stairs before being taken away in a military jeep in a scene captured on video.
  - Awad’s reporting for Drop Site has covered escalating violence by Israeli settlers across the West Bank, including the burning of a mosque in Qusra, south of Nablus, and an attack in Masafer Yatta last week that wounded five Palestinians and burned four homes.
  - With his detention, the number of Palestinian journalists held in Israeli prisons has risen to 40, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.
  - Israel has killed more than 260 journalists since it began its genocide in Gaza, two of whom died in Israeli prisons.
- Conditions for prisoners in Ganot deteriorating rapidly: Living and humanitarian conditions for Palestinians imprisoned in Ganot prison in southern Israel are deteriorating rapidly, the Palestinian government’s Commission for Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said in a Wednesday report. 
  - Ministry officials who visited several prisons reported overcrowding, regular beatings, and insufficient supplies.
  - The report also noted a lack of access to basic hygiene routines and supplies. At Ganot, prisoners wear the same clothing for up to two weeks, go without access to washing machines for the same period, and are forced to share razors and nail clippers.
- UN: Thousands in Gaza still await medical evacuation: Thousands of patients in the Gaza Strip are still awaiting medical evacuation despite the ceasefire, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization said on Tuesday. 
  - The spokesperson noted the difficulties of evacuation in remarks to reporters and said they were conducted three or four times per week, as Israel continues to restrict movement through the Rafah crossing.
  - Around 15,000 Palestinians in Gaza require medical treatment abroad, according to the Strip’s Health Ministry.
- Israel continues to ravage the occupied West Bank: 
  - Nablus: Israeli settlers continued to besiege the Qusra home of the Palestinian-American Abu Rida family for a fourth consecutive day on Wednesday, according to WAFA, circling the property and preventing entry or exit, blocking the road to the property with rocks, and attempting to enter the home. The settlers have attempted to seize the property for months, often with the backing of the Israeli military.
  - Hebron: Israeli authorities closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron on Wednesday, preventing worshippers from reaching it, while conducting raids in the area. Additionally on Wednesday, Israeli forces bulldozed a home in Hebron without notice or explanation. On Tuesday, settlers demolished a Palestinian house, leaving nine people homeless, and filled in a water well in the Bedouin community of Yatta.
  - Bethlehem: Israeli forces demolished a three-story residential building in the village of Ma’sara on Wednesday morning.
  - East Jerusalem: Israeli settlers continued to work on a settlement expansion project on pastoral land near the Ma’azi Jaba Bedouin community, north of East Jerusalem, on Wednesday, WAFA reported. Separately on Wednesday, Israeli forces demolished a home in Silwan, according to the Jerusalem governorate.
  - Tubas: Israeli settlers vandalized the main water supply line of the Ras al-Ahmar community in the Tubas governorate, cutting off water to 30 Palestinian families.
- Security Council holds West Bank meeting, official says area “at breaking point”: At a meeting of the United Nations Security Council, UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov warned on Tuesday that the occupied West Bank was at a “breaking point,” with settler attacks across Areas A, B, and C increasing at a rapid clip. 
  - Alakbarov told the Council that, as of August 10, Israel had killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank, including 18 children. “The pattern is clear,” he said, “Palestinians are being forcibly displaced across the West Bank before settlers seize the vacated land.”
  - At the meeting, UNICEF also noted that Israel had killed 174 Palestinian children in the West Bank—or more than one per week—since January 2024. UNICEF also noted that at least 355 Palestinian children from the occupied West Bank are currently being held in Israeli military detention, according to the Israeli Prison Service—the highest number in eight years.
- NCAG meets with UN: The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the sole Palestinian body operating under Trump’s “Board of Peace,” convened a joint meeting with UN agencies on Tuesday, hoping to align their strategies and to establish mechanisms for coordinating relief, recovery, and reconstruction.
Lebanon
- Israel continues attacks in Lebanon despite “ceasefire” framework: 
  - Israeli forces bombed a four-story public school in the center of the village of Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah on Wednesday, according to the country’s National News Agency (NNA).
  - An Israeli drone struck a religious Ashura procession on the Kafra–al-Asi road in the Tyre (Sour) district, wounding several, the NNA reported.
  - Israeli forces conducted additional bombing operations in Haddatha and Beit Yahoun on Wednesday, the NNA reported, calling the second of these a “massive explosion.”
  - The Lebanese army said Israeli forces blew up the municipal building in Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah in Nabatieh, along with the town’s public school, health clinic, children’s nursery and several homes. It added that Israel is continuing its “destructive approach” in southern Lebanon, saying the attacks were hindering the army’s deployment and the return of residents.
- Lebanon becomes first Arab country to abolish death penalty: Lebanon’s parliament voted Tuesday to abolish the death penalty, making it the first Arab country to replace the sentence with life imprisonment with “aggravated” hard labor, AP reported. The law is expected to benefit thousands of prisoners, detainees and wanted individuals and is aimed primarily at easing severe prison overcrowding, including cases of detainees held for years without trial. 
  - Official figures put Lebanon’s prison population at 6,268 as of March 30, while the National Human Rights Commission reported prison overcrowding at 300% in 2025.
