And I appreciated it for a number of reasons, including the fact that you drew on this John Bistline paper, who’s a researcher at Watershed, trying to estimate the emissions intensity of AI, which was in turn covered by my colleague, Emily Panacorvo. So always great to see heat map in the mix. But your general takeaway from this paper and also from your own estimates was that AI, probably at this point, given how we use it, is much more emissions intensive than maybe early estimates or is somewhat more emissions intensive than early estimates and you were able to put some error bars around how we should think about electricity use associated with both chatbot ai and then also agentic and cloud code style ai and describe a little bit what you think the discourse is missing right now around those topics and why you think speaking of estimates coming in on the high end why some of the more popular estimates around the emissions intensity of AI may underestimate its emissions.
So when you’re looking at AI energy use, there’s sort of top-down and bottom-up approaches you can take. I think the top-down numbers are broadly right, and those are the ones that give like, I don’t know, 15% of U.S. electricity use by 2030 going to AI data centers on the high end. I’m not arguing that estimates like those are too low. What this piece was more about is, what is the impact of me as an individual using AI tools? And there, the numbers that were published last year in 2025 by folks like Google or by OpenAI are not very realistic to the way people are actually using AI today. So these numbers that were published in 2025 were that AI per prompt, and by prompt, they mean typing something in a chat GPT text box and hitting enter and getting a response without a reasoning model, important distinction. So just one shot. But those take about 0.3 watts of energy, which really isn’t much, right? At 0.3 watts, you could do many, many, many thousands or tens of thousands of AI prompts and still have much lower impact than, you know. Running your air conditioner in the afternoon or, you know, driving to work.
That’s less than how a light bulb used to be. So if you didn’t feel bad about adding a single new lamp to your home, then you shouldn’t feel bad, so to speak, about using AI under that estimate. Yeah.
But the problem, of course, is that some people are still using AI that way, but increasingly AI is being used in an agentic form. And that more means that you give AI a set of instructions or a goal to achieve. And then AI goes off and does many, many, many, things to try to achieve that goal. AI agents are, at least in the corporate world and the software engineering and scientific world, the vast majority of AI use today. And those agents make both much more complicated calls than the prompts would suggest and many, many more calls. And so when you look at the actual energy use of these AI agents, it’s something on the order of 600 times larger per prompt than the traditional, like, type something in a chat box and got to get an immediate response. And so that does end up adding up. I actually looked at two months of my own AI use because I had local logs of all of the numbers there.
When you say local AI use, these are calls you’re making locally to ChatGPT or Claude that you’ve retained a record for but the ai is still being run on an external device you don’t have a power meter hooked up to your desktop
Yeah my desktop is using next to nothing this is some data center spinning up to process the call i made on my local cloud code but i found that on average i was using about three kilowatt hours a day for my agentic energy use which is the equivalent of running two refrigerators so that’s not nothing in big days when i was really doing some complicated like geospatial analysis or big data crunching exercise, I was using upwards of 10 kilowatt-hours per day. So maybe a third of the typical US household energy is just going to AI agents. And if you annualize that over the entire year, you end up with numbers that they’re not crazy. So for an entire year, my estimate is that my agentic AI energy use is about 1.1 megawatt-hours. If you convert that to CO2, again, using sort of a roughly average grid intensity, It’s about 370 kilograms of CO2. So that’s roughly half of a transcontinental flight. So again, it’s not enormous in terms of my overall emissions, but it’s also not trivial, like some of these initial estimates that came out last year would suggest.
Carbon emissions with average U.S. grid intensity or with the likely kind of it’s all coming from gas that...
All coming from gas and average U.S. grid intensity are not that far apart at the moment.
Yes.
Yeah. So this is using a bit of location-based analysis, but it’s pretty close to the all-gas assumption now. Where I’ve gotten some criticism there is people who said, well, if you account for the fact that these AI companies are buying RECs to cover their data center energy use by building clean energy elsewhere, even if it’s not directly powering the data center, then the number is probably lower. Which, you know, might be fair if they actually disclosed what those numbers would be, I would be happy to use them. But unfortunately, at the moment, AI companies are really not telling us much about the actual energy use of their products. And so we’re having to infer all this with very indirect methods. One of the main takeaways from this piece should be a plea for AI companies to be more transparent and actually tell us how much energy their systems are using.
I think this is very striking, particularly by Anthropic, which I think has published absolutely no estimates per token of its emissions intensity or energy use, even though it’s the quote unquote kind of good AI company. We just are kind of completely in the dark about what Claude uses. And in fact, we know that Anthropic is contracted with one of the Colossus data centers built by XAI, which is one of the worst offenders in terms of particularly emissions-intensive generation.
We’re going to have to leave it there. As El Niño continues to develop, maybe we’ll have you back to talk about just how bad it is. Zeke Hausfather, thank you so much for joining us on Shift Key.
Thanks, Rob. It was a great conversation.
And that will do it for us this week, but we’ll be back next week with a new episode of ShiftKey. Until then, Shift Key is a production of Heatmap News. Our editors are Jillian Goodman and Nico Lauricella. Multimedia editing and audio engineering is by Jacob Lambert and by Nick Woodbury. Our music’s by Adam Kromelow. Thanks so much for listening. We’ll see you next week.
Boston-based startup Reservoir has raised an $8 million seed round to commercialize heat pump-powered water heaters.
There are plenty of ways to leverage everyday household appliances to shift electricity demand and free up capacity on the grid. But when energy nerds talk about these opportunities, they’re mostly focused on distributed energy resources like smart thermostats, residential batteries, and electric vehicle chargers. Water heaters — the vast majority of which are not internet connected — rarely enter the conversation.
Boston-based startup Reservoir wants to change that, raising a $8 million seed round to bring its sexier, techier heat pump water heaters to market. Asymmetric Capital Partners led the round, alongside Founder Collective and the climate-focused investor MCJ.
The startup has already installed its water heaters in nearly 100 homes around Boston. Each unit pairs an onboard computer with a heat pump, allowing it to learn a household’s hot water habits so it can begin preheating hours in advance of, say, your morning shower. That long lead time matters, as a heat pump can take five or six hours to warm up a standard 50-gallon tank. But if your schedule shifts and you need hot water at an atypical time, the unit comes equipped with backup resistance heating elements, allowing it to heat the tank quickly using the same technology many conventional water heaters do.
The company’s CEO, Luke Winston-Almanzar, was inspired to start the company when he realized that his water heater consumed more energy per year than it took to charge his electric car, but was dumber than his air fryer or watch.
“Most people don’t realize the water heater is the second biggest use of energy in the home. It’s almost 20%,” he told me, coming in behind space heating and cooling, which account for around half of a household’s total energy consumption. He saw an opportunity to help bring smart, energy efficient water heaters into the digital age, much the way Nest did for thermostats.
Simply switching to a heat pump water heater can already cut energy use by about 75% compared with standard electric models, which account for about half the nation’s fleet. And while most heat pump models now come equipped with internet connectivity and remote adjustment mechanisms, the startup’s predictive software is what truly sets it apart. While other units simply hold water at a consistent temperature, Reservoir squeezes out additional energy savings by only heating when it anticipates hot water will actually be needed, Winston-Almanzar told me. Ultimately, this adds up to an average $800 per year in customer savings compared to standard electric tanks, and around $150 for gas-powered tanks, according to the company’s estimates.
Scale that up to thousands of households, and water heaters become a grid resource that can participate in demand response programs and virtual power plants. “You get a smart water heater in homes — you can save people money, you can increase their comfort. But then you get 50,000 of them, and they’re connected, and you can actually offset Elon Musk’s data center,” Winston-Almanzar explained.
Because water heaters store thermal rather than electrical energy, they can’t send electricity back to the grid like residential battery storage systems can. But they can still shift when they consume electricity. For example, Reservoir can heat water in the early morning when demand on the grid is low and hold it until people start waking up and showering. Or for households that use more hot water in the evening, the system can heat up around midday when there’s lots of cheap, clean power on the grid. During times of peak demand, it can simply pause its heating cycle, drawing on the water it’s already stored.
While Reservoir hasn’t yet integrated its systems with a virtual power plant provider that could compensate customers for helping to alleviate strain on the grid, Winston-Almanzar sees this as a near-term opportunity. “What I’m sprinting towards is getting 1,000 units installed in Massachusetts because that gets us to the megawatt-hour-scale of thermal storage,” he told me, explaining that’s when VPP integration will start to make sense for a specific region.
Today, the startup’s base model retails for less than $4,000 fully installed, compared to $3,000 to $6,000 for a standard electric water heater, and includes all of Reservoir’s predictive capabilities. The company also offers a more feature-rich $5,450 model that has a “Party Mode,” which effectively stretches the capacity of a 50-gallon tank to deliver up to 150 gallons of hot water on high-demand days, such as when a household is hosting guests. This model can also proactively adjust the system when water pipes are at risk of freezing and offers “no-wait” showers, using a recirculation pump to deliver hot water instantaneously, without having to let the tap run first.
Those prices include the $1,050 rebate available for heat pump water heaters in Massachusetts, where Reservoir’s early installations are concentrated. While the Trump administration axed the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit, which covered 30% of the costs of eligible units up to $2,000, Winston-Almanzar says state-level incentives are helping fill the gap. The company has already expanded into Maine and New Hampshire, which offer their own rebates, and plans to enter additional major metro markets such as New York, Washington DC, Seattle, and San Francisco.
The company is also betting on its installation process as a competitive advantage. Rather than relying entirely on third-party contractors, Reservoir employs an in-house team of young, digitally native plumbers to install its systems — a team it expects will grow substantially as the company scales.
Ultimately, if Reservoir succeeds in becoming the Nest of water heaters, Winston-Almanzar predicts systems like his will eventually replace smart thermostats in VPP programs. “If you have a battery for where you need electrons moving, and you have a tank of water for when you need just heat moving, homeowners don’t even need to feel it,” he explained. While adjusting a customer’s thermostat can immediately impact their comfort, changing a water heater’s background operations will go largely unnoticed, he argued, making them a better option for VPP integration.
Turning one of a home’s largest energy loads into a giant grid battery that saves customers money certainly seems like a good bet. But it’s still early days. Reservoir will have to prove, through many thousands more installations, that the humble water heater truly has what it takes to become one of the grid’s most valuable distributed resources.

sources.news_title: Francesca Hong's Wisconsin Defeat Exposes DSA's Flaws
Crowley goes from dropping out to winning Wisconsin Democratic nomination
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – David Crowley went from dropping out of the Wisconsin governor’s race to being the Democratic nominee.
The Milwaukee County Executive holds a more than 3,000-vote lead with 98% of votes reporting and is the projected winner in a close race against state Rep. Francesca Hong, a Democratic socialist, to take on Republican Tom Tiffany in the Nov. 3 general election.
“From day one, this campaign has been about what comes next for Wisconsin: making life more affordable, strengthening our schools, creating good-paying jobs, and making sure opportunity reaches every corner of our state,” Crowley campaign manager Darren Randolph said in a statement.
Crowley becomes the projected winner after absentee votes from Milwaukee County’s Central Count were added to the totals just before 1:30 a.m. on Wednesday.
Hong was a distinct leader in polls heading into the race as Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez and former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes dropped out late but remained on ballots.
“The fight continues no matter what,” Hong said before ending her watch party before the Milwaukee County Central Count numbers arrived.
Republican Tom Tiffany was declared the winner of his primary for Wisconsin governor in the minutes after polls closed.
Tiffany held 95.3% of the early votes while opponent Andy Manske had 4.6%.
"I want to thank Wisconsinites across our state for putting their trust in me,” Tiffany said in a statement. “This fight is bigger than any one party. It’s bigger than any one candidate. This fight is about Wisconsin and protecting the state we know and love. It’s about lowering property taxes, returning the surplus to you, getting utility costs under control, and letting hardworking Wisconsinites keep more of what they earn. Let’s move Wisconsin forward, together."
Tiffany said that there aren't huge differences between the candidates on the Democratic side of the primary.
"I’ve said all along that there’s not a dime’s worth of difference between these Democrat candidates, and David Crowley proved my point when he admitted there aren’t many policy differences between him and a socialist," Tiffany said in a statement. "His record in Milwaukee County shows exactly what Wisconsin would get: mismanage the government, run up the bill, and raise your taxes to pay for it. Wisconsin doesn’t need more of the same failed policies. I’m running to lower costs, restore accountability in Madison, and expand opportunity across our state."

sources.news_title: Crowley Stuns In WI, Beating Socialist In Dem Governor Primary
sources.text:
Wisconsin Democrats on Tuesday disregarded the polls and narrowly rejected an avowed socialist as their nominee for governor in the Badger State’s nationally-watched primary election.
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who dropped out of the race late only to be coaxed back in by the so-called Democratic Party “establishment,” defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong by razor thin margins.
Per usual, Crowley’s Milwaukee County faced a ballot count delay, a stoppage that dragged out the tally for hours and was once again blamed on “human error.” It’s another in a string of election night messes for Milwaukee, Wisconsin’s most-populated — and election integrity challenged city.
With 98.4 percent of the vote in just before 2 a.m., Crowley led by just four-tenths of a percentage point, or just over 3,000 votes. The New York Times finally called the race for Crowley just before 3 a.m. local time.
‘Best Candidate to Lose the Race’
Crowley’s narrow victory was a stunner, with Hong heading into election day holding a commanding lead in the polls and plenty of pundits calling the time of death on Crowley’s 11th-hour reentry into the race. Reports of the less far-left candidate’s political demise were premature.
The big guns of said establishment were sweating long into the wee hours of the morning, as they watched Crowley hold on to win. It was a near-miss for a party that dreaded the daunting task of running a radical socialist with an inexhaustible supply of crazy tweets and crazier policy positions. The GOP’s candidate, Rep. Tom Tiffany, is a down-to-earth conservative who represents the Northwoods 7th Congressional District that Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy previously served.
Tiffany cruised to primary win over a challenger who grabbed just 4 1/2 percent of the vote.
Two-term Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat who supports many of the same “woke 1.0” policies that Hong has championed, helped resurrect Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley’s moribund campaign just a few weeks before election day.
“Among other people’s necks who are on the line tonight are Gov. Evers, who went all-in over the last 10 days or so making appearances [for Crowley],” Republican Party of Wisconsin Chairman Brian Schimming told me Tuesday on the Jason Goch Show in Milwaukee.
Evers earlier this month told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that he didn’t think the radical Hong could win in November’s general election. And the governor who fought for moms to be described as “inseminated persons” in state documents, took a subtle shot at the socialist’s ability to govern the state, saying after eight years in office he wants to “leave Wisconsin in good hands when someone else takes over.”
Some of Hong’s most high profile Democratic Socialists of America comrades refused to endorse her. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the godfather of American socialism, and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, busy these days freezing her eggs, both balked at giving their political blessing to Hong.
“You know, it’s the only time that I know that the governor — Tony Evers — the Republican Governors Association and Turning Point USA have ever been on the same page: in thinking that Francesca Hong is the best candidate to lose this race,” Crowley said in an interview last week with Politico at a local tavern in Sheboygan.
‘Cancel Thanksgiving’
In one of the more ridiculous political reinventions since Millard Fillmore jumped on the Know Nothing Party bus in 1856, Hong spent much of the campaign pretending she’s nothing like her social media posts. The radical’s long record of extreme tweets and socialist policy positions have dogged her throughout a Dem Party primary exploding with scandal.
Perhaps Hong’s most cringeworthy flip-flop involved one of America’s most cherished holidays.
“Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621,” the critical race theory-spewing socialist opined on Twitter on Nov. 16, 2020 — in the crux of Covid. “If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed Indigenous folx and women so be it.”
Fearing backlash from Democratic Party voters who haven’t plunged headfirst into the DSA’s radical waters, Hong has awkwardly attempted to distance herself from herself. She no longer wants to cancel Thanksgiving.
“I actually love it,” the shameless gubernatorial candidate recently told Politico.
Hong went all-in on the Black Lives Matter fiery but mostly peaceful movement, demanding policymakers defund — and abolish — the police. She posted the same about federal immigration law enforcement. Hong told supporters that her “perfect world would be a world without prisons,” according to audio obtained by the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. Her “tax the rich” tax-and-spend proposal would hit Wisconsin with the highest personal income tax rate in the nation — higher than the current champion, California — by nearly 4 percentage points. Like fellow socialist, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Hong “wrote a bill to create publicly-owned grocery stores.” She’s an absolute hawk on protecting sex changes for children and “students’ preferred pronouns.”
More Milwaukee Mess
The long wait for election results has become standard operating procedure for Wisconsin elections, mucked up by the latest round of irregularities from Milwaukee election officials.
As ABC Milwaukee affiliate WISN reported, Milwaukee Election Commission Executive Director Paulina Gutierrez “discovered five of the nine flash drives brought to central count had the audit log downloaded and not the results.”
Election officials had to head back to central count in Milwaukee and download the results for a second time from five ballot tabulators. The results were to be “reuploaded” at the Milwaukee County Courthouse, Gutierrez told WISN.
Based on the unofficial count, when the final Milwaukee County vote was finally tallied, Crowley had won the county by nearly 2,400 votes.
In other key primary races Tuesday …
‘A Battle for the Soul of America’
Wisconsin’s nationally-watched 3rd Congressional District contest will be a rematch from 2024. Democrat Rebecca Cooke, who identifies as a moderate the same way the fellow formerly known as Tim McBride identifies as a Delaware congresswoman, will face off against two-term incumbent Republican Derrick Van Orden, who beat Cooke by 11,000 votes in their last matchup. The 3rd is one of a handful of races Democrats believe they can knock off in November in their pursuit to take back the House.
“Rebecca Cooke is exactly who the national Democrats wanted, an anointed candidate they know will carry water for the socialists who have taken over their party,” Van Orden said in a press release. “This election is about what kind of country we are going to leave to our children and grandchildren. It is a battle for the soul of America.”
Trump Power
In the race to replace Tiffany, Duffy’s son-in-law Michael Alfonso crushed his competitors, showing again the power of President Donald Trump’s endorsement. Alfonso is the odds-on favorite to win the general in the ruby red district.
The 26-year-old Alfonso entered Tuesday with a sizable lead in the polls over second-place finisher Kevin Hermening, a financial adviser and Marine veteran who was one of the 52 captives in the Iran Hostage Crisis. The four-person primary grew increasingly contentious, with attack ads labeling frontrunner Alfonso a “nepo baby.”
Didn’t matter. Duffy’s son-in-law had the backing of conservative stalwart organizations Turning Point USA and Moms for Liberty and members of Wisconsin Republican congressional delegation. But the Trump endorsement proved powerful once again, as the president wracks up an impressive success record this election cycle.
Trump’s Truth Social account was filled Tuesday with celebratory posts of the endorsement wins he collected.
‘Dying to Run Against’
The president’s choice for Republican governor in blue state Minnesota didn’t fare so well. MyPillow peddler Mike Lindell, who built a lead in the polls, lost to State House Speaker Lisa Demuth in the race to replace TDS Democrat and fraud scandal patriarch Gov. Tim Walz. DeMuth also defeated Minnesota businessman Kendall Qualls, who picked up the endorsement of the Minnesota GOP.
DeMuth will face Democrat Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who sailed to victory Tuesday for her party’s gubernatorial nomination.
Minnesota Democrats stayed true to their leftward lurch, delivering a primary victory to far-left Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the Democratic primary for Senate. Flanagan defeated the left-proclaimed “moderate” in the race, Rep. Angie Craig. Craig had the money and the backing of outgoing senator and Trump Derangement Syndrome sufferer Tina Smith, as well as Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Sanders of Vermont — the “establishment.”
Flanagan, who constantly reminded identity politics Democrats that she would be Minnesota’s first “Native woman” to be elected to the U.S. Senate, ingratiated herself with Minnesota’s Somali community when she showed up at a Mosque last December wearing a hijab. It was a gesture of solidarity as federal investigators stepped up investigations into the state’s welfare fraud scandal, which to a significant extent involved members of the Somali community.
Craig argued that “Republicans are dying to run against” Flanagan because she was front and center in the state’s welfare fraud scandal. That didn’t seem to matter to Minnesota Democrats, who chose the lieutenant governor by a wide margin.
The Republican running against her will be former sportscaster Michele Tafoya, who coasted to victory.
South Carolina Runoff Set
In South Carolina’s GOP Senate primary, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darlene Graham, appointed to serve out the rest of his term, will face Rep. Ralph Norman in an Aug. 25 runoff.
Darlene Graham, endorsed by President Trump, won 33 percent of the total vote, while Norman grabbed 25 percent, according to unofficial results as of early Wednesday morning. The packed field of 10 candidates, including Norman, Rep. Russell Fry and former Gov. Mark Sanford.
The winner of the runoff will go up against Democrat Annie Andrews, who won her party’s nomination in June.

sources.news_title: Democratic socialist falls in Wisconsin; Colombia races to find quake survivors
sources.text:
David Crowley pulled off a surprise win over democratic socialist Francesca Hong in Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary, putting a dent in the progressive wing’s recent run of primary victories.
Plus, rescuers continue to dig through the rubble following Colombia’s devastating earthquake, with more than 200 people dead and thousands still missing as the search for survivors continues.
And former American Marine Robert Gilman is back in the U.S. after more than four years in Russian custody, but his release comes with serious concerns about the condition of his health.
These stories and more highlight your Unbiased Updates for Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026.
Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.™
Point phone camera here
Crowley defeats Hong in Wisconsin as Graham, Norman head to South Carolina runoff
Results from Tuesday’s primaries are in, including a comeback win in Wisconsin and a runoff for Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley has won the Democratic nomination for governor of Wisconsin, defeating Democratic socialist Francesca Hong.
It’s a striking turnaround for Crowley, who dropped out of the race last month, then jumped back in after another leading Democrat dropped out.
Gov. Tony Evers then endorsed Crowley in the closing days of the race, helping Democrats coalesce around his candidacy.
Hong had led in polling, and her loss cuts short another test of how far the party’s progressive wing can extend its recent primary wins into a presidential battleground.
Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany also won his party’s nomination for governor, setting up a Crowley-Tiffany matchup in November.
And in South Carolina, Lindsey Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham, and Rep. Ralph Norman are headed to a runoff later this month in the special Republican primary for Graham’s former Senate seat.
Both talked overnight about the sudden, short campaign and the two weeks still ahead.
“I have buried my precious brother, I have taken on the role of the United States senator, and I have had this brutal campaign schedule, and I am still standing,” Graham said. “If that doesn’t tell you I am a strong person and a fighter, nothing will. So I think I can handle the next two weeks.”
“How unexpected this was to have Lindsey Graham not here,” Norman said. “He just, he’s a fixture you thought he would be here. And that being said, it was, when you looked at the landscape, it was a short time frame to put together a campaign.”
And one more upset in Minnesota.
Republican voters chose state house speaker Lisa Demuth over President Donald Trump ally Mike Lindell for their party’s nomination for governor.
Demuth will face democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar in November.
Pakistan says US, Iran reportedly closer to deal as Trump still claims control of Strait of Hormuz
Pakistan’s defense minister says the U.S. and Iran may be getting closer to a deal, saying the two sides are near “some sort of an arrangement.”
It comes despite Trump once again claiming the U.S. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz and saying the situation with Iran is going “absolutely fine.”
But Trump also made clear he does not trust Tehran’s representatives, and once again left open the possibility of renewed military action.
“I don’t trust Iran. Why? Are you saying I trust the right? I’m the last person to trust the rest,” Trump said. “They’ve lied to me constantly. We have total control over the Hormuz Strait right now. They don’t have control. We have total control. We own it. And at some point, maybe they’ll do something and then they get blown away. But right now, we’re in a very good position.”
Iran, however, insists it controls security in the strait and says it will remain closed until the U.S. meets its conditions.
Tehran is also rejecting Trump’s counter-demand for compensation as part of any peace deal.
Meanwhile, Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen say they targeted a ship carrying Saudi military equipment in the Bab Al-Mandab strait on Tuesday.
That claim has not been verified, and Yemen’s internationally recognized government says the ship was carrying food supplies.
Six people were killed in the attack, including three Pakistani nationals.
It’s part of a new escalation by the Houthis, who have also attacked the government-held port city of Mokha and other parts of Yemen in recent days.
And in the Gulf of Oman, U.S. Central Command says a Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the engine room of a Panamanian-flagged cargo ship after it ignored repeated warnings and tried to break the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports.
CENTCOM says it’s the third ship disabled since the blockade resumed last month.
Colombia searches for survivors as US sends $15.5 million in aid
In Colombia, rescuers are digging through rubble by hand, racing to find people still alive after Monday’s devastating 7.4-magnitude earthquake.
The quake knocked down buildings, damaged roads and left thousands of families searching for loved ones.
And the death toll is still shifting.
Colombia’s president put the number of dead at 181, while the country’s public ministry later said at least 224 people have been killed.
More than 1,300 people have been reported injured, and more than 3,000 are missing.
In Cali alone, the mayor says 95 people were killed and 949 injured, with another 239 believed to be trapped in the rubble.
At least 86 people have been rescued there so far.
Crews worked through the night, in some places forming human chains to move bricks and concrete, then stopping to listen for signs of life.
And there have been rescues.
In Cali, one volunteer described hearing someone whistle back from beneath a collapsed building. Rescuers later pulled out a man and a baby.
President Abelardo de la Espriella, sworn in just three days before the quake, has declared a national disaster.
And the U.S. response is now underway.
A disaster assistance response team is heading to Colombia, and the Trump administration has committed $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food and other relief.
Russia releases former US Marine from prison after more than four years
A former U.S. Marine returned to American soil Tuesday after more than four years in a Russian prison, amid mounting fears he might not survive. The Russian government released Robert Gilman, citing humanitarian grounds, as both the U.S. and Russia describe it.
Trump said he discussed Gilman’s release with Vladimir Putin and that Russia asked for no one in return. Therefore, no prisoner swap took place.
The president also spoke with Gilman on his flight home and said the 32-year-old had one request upon landing: a great cheeseburger.
The lighter moment belies the seriousness of Gilman’s condition. His advocates said he spent weeks in what they described as a dissociative stupor and was later moved to a Russian hospital, where he was fed through a tube. Russia arrested him in 2022 after he was accused of kicking a police officer on a train.
Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey, a Democrat, worked with Gilman’s family for two years to secure his release, but said it took far too long.
“While this news is deeply welcome, it is a tragedy that it took Robert’s near-death condition for this case to receive the attention which it required for his release to be negotiated,” he said. “Because of bipartisan work, Robert Gilman is free. Robert Gilman is heading back to his family.”
Gilman’s family and U.S. officials have accused Russia of abusing him in custody. He’s now expected to undergo medical and psychological treatment at a U.S. military hospital in Texas.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X that the U.S. continues to seek the immediate return of other Americans held in Russia, including wrongfully detained American Stephen Hubbard.
Gilman is the third former U.S. Marine detained by Russia in recent years, following Trevor Reed and Paul Whelan, both of whom were eventually freed in prisoner swaps.
White House asks DOJ to explore renewed charges against former Olympian in Reflecting Pool case
The White House has asked the Justice Department to assess whether it can bring a new case against the man accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. This follows federal prosecutors’ decision to drop the original case, saying the damage wasn’t vandalism.
The Wall Street Journal was the first to report that White House officials have asked the Justice Department to explore whether David Hearn could be prosecuted again.
Federal prosecutors initially accused Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, of removing part of the new coating on the bottom of the reflecting pool. But they later dropped the felony case after new information showed the damage was caused by what they called a “botched installation,” not vandalism.
Trump has publicly blasted U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro for dropping the case and urged her to revisit the decision.
Now, after prodding from the White House, the Justice Department is considering whether there’s another path forward — possibly a misdemeanor case.
A judge is expected to decide whether the original case should be dismissed “with prejudice,” which could prevent the Justice Department from charging Hearn again over the same alleged conduct.
This now falls to a Justice Department with a new leader. Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general Monday and has said the president has both the right and the duty to weigh in on Justice Department matters.
Rare Mario games discovered after decades in storage
A Wisconsin pop-culture store owner told Nintendo collector Jason Ganos he had an old box of Super Mario cartridges in storage. It turns out they weren’t just old.
The box held 97 pristine copies of Super Mario Bros./Duck Hunt — and Ganos discovered they were an ultra-rare variant produced in 1993, two years after the bundle was believed to have been discontinued.
“This happened to be a new variant of Super Mario Brothers. Not just any new variant; we found out that it was the last known production date for this game. Previously, they thought that they stopped manufacturing these in 1991. These were made in 1993, and that was long after they discontinued that bundle. The Super Nintendo was out at that point.”
Jason Ganos, owner og Nintendo Wire
And they’re not just rare; they’re in remarkable condition.
Five of the 97 received a perfect 10 from a professional sports authenticator, according to Ganos, something that had never happened before to an NES cartridge.
Most of the collection goes up for auction starting Friday. Ganos called the entire discovery “serendipitous” and said he won’t even guess what it will sell for. But regardless, he’s about to find out.
More from Straight Arrow:
Reality TV shows force contestants offline. Experts say it’s good for them
When Derrick Kosinski arrives on set for MTV’s “The Challenge,” he clings to his phone, delaying the inevitable: the moment when he has to hand over the device before participating in what could be months of competitive challenges.
“You’re trying to hold onto it as long as you can,” Kosinski, a 15-time contestant on “The Challenge” and host of the “Challenge Mania” podcast, told Straight Arrow. “You’re trying to scroll as long as you can, and tell your loved ones, like, ‘I’m out. I love you, later, this is it. I’m giving my phone away.’”
But once it’s out of his hands? Kosinski says it’s not so bad.
“The game kind of begins, and it’s almost like … I think it’s a relief,” Kosinski said. “Then, it’s like going back to what it was like back in the day when there weren’t all these phones, when you were a kid — I get to play this really dope game.”

sources.news_title: Trump-Backed Candidates Face Key Tests as Primaries Unfold
sources.text:
Voters in several states headed to the polls Tuesday for a round of primaries that could reshape key races ahead of the 2026 midterms, with President Donald Trump’s influence over Republican voters facing another test.
According to Fox News, in South Carolina, Trump backed Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, in a crowded Republican primary to fill her brother’s Senate seat.
She had been appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve the remainder of the term following Graham’s death.
Her Republican rivals included Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry, along with former Gov. Mark Sanford.
The biggest Democratic battles were unfolding farther north, where Wisconsin and Minnesota featured contests that could reveal the direction of the party heading into the general election.
In Wisconsin, state Rep. Francesca Hong emerged as the leading Democratic contender for governor.
The 37-year-old former chef and single mother has drawn support from prominent progressives while facing criticism over past social media posts about policing and Thanksgiving.
Hong has since said she does not support defunding or abolishing police departments and has described her earlier comments as positions she has moved beyond.
Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany is heavily favored for the GOP nomination and has Trump's endorsement. Tiffany has framed the race as a fight against what he calls socialism, saying Wisconsin could serve as a "firewall" against the political left.
The Democratic primary has been unsettled by several candidates leaving the race, while Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley returned after previously suspending his campaign. Gov. Tony Evers endorsed Crowley during the closing stretch of the contest.
Republicans have also spent money supporting Hong's candidacy, viewing her as a potentially weaker opponent for the general election.
Minnesota offered another test of the Democratic Party's internal divide. Progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and more moderate Rep. Angie Craig were competing for the Democratic Senate nomination to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith.
A Republican win in Minnesota would be significant, as the GOP has not captured a Senate election in the state in more than two decades.
Republican Michele Tafoya entered the primary as a leading candidate, with several others also competing.
Trump's endorsement record was another storyline in South Carolina.
His preferred candidate for governor, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, won the most votes in the initial Republican primary but later lost the runoff to Attorney General Alan Wilson after Trump also endorsed Wilson.
Other contests Tuesday included Connecticut's Democratic gubernatorial primary, Vermont's races for governor and several special congressional primaries in Alabama.
The results could offer an early look at the candidates and political factions best positioned for the battles ahead.

sources.news_title: Democratic Socialists Hit a Wall in Wisconsin
Francesca Hong lost. Here’s what it means for progressives.
sources.text:
It turns out there is a limit to how far left Democrats are willing to go with a crucial swing state on the line.
Francesca Hong lost. Here’s what it means for progressives.
The socialist candidate for governor fell short Tuesday as concerns about her electability carried the day.
Francesca Hong ran up against that wall on Tuesday, falling short in her race against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination in Wisconsin.
He’ll go up against Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Republican backed by President Donald Trump and closely associated with his MAGA movement, setting up a major contrast in a state where elections are often decided by paper-thin margins.
Had Hong won, she would have had a chance to become the first democratic socialist governor in any state in US history. And Hong was the story of the election for most of the last month: She led recent polls by a double-digit margin, and Crowley’s campaign was considered a last-second rescue mission by party leaders — he had previously dropped out of the race, and only rejoined it last month with Gov. Tony Evers’s encouragement after other candidates faltered.
Despite his earlier stumbles, however, Crowley managed to consolidate Democratic support amid widespread concerns about Hong’s viability in a general election.
Hong’s rise and fall showcased multiple trends in the party — the growing appeal of progressive populism, the struggles of center-left party leaders to contain it, and an ongoing debate about electability that ultimately proved too much for her to overcome.
The issue that helped propel Hong’s campaign
Hong, 37, is a chef by trade and first ran for state assembly in 2020 while struggling to keep her ramen restaurant afloat during the pandemic. She tapped into the same well of progressive activism that’s powered other insurgent campaigns this year, positioning herself as a candidate who would aim higher in office than her opponents.
“Incrementalism is irresponsible,” she told Vox’s Andrew Prokop last month. “Pushing for the middle or the moderate has not yielded us the wins that we need.”
But state political experts credited one issue in particular for helping her stand out the most: data centers.
Hong was an early and vocal opponent just as public opposition was beginning to surge. Running on a pledge to “Control-Alt-Delete” the AI buildout, she pledged to cut off tax incentives and implement a moratorium on new projects.
The rest of the field imploded
Though Hong’s populist-left politics dominated the headlines, the story of her rise was also about a cascading series of failures among the rest of the Democratic field.
Just as Democratic leaders hoped to consolidate behind a more conventional candidate to head off Hong, things started going off the rails in the final weeks of the contest, leaving them little time to course-correct.
In July, Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race just as her campaign was gaining some traction, citing campaign finance irregularities that made it impossible to continue.
That left former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who lost a close Senate race in 2022, as Hong’s only significant rival. But Evers, concerned about Barnes’s viability, encouraged Crowley to reenter the race after he had already dropped out, and then endorsed his revived campaign.
Barnes and Crowley split the vote in polls while Hong surged — but then Barnes dropped out just as the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel revealed it was investigating allegations of sexual misconduct.
Republicans, meanwhile, were happy to take advantage of the mess to try to build momentum for Hong, who they saw as a weaker opponent. A group associated with the Republican Governors Association spent over $3 million on “attack” ads to help elevate her profile with Democratic primary voters.
With just weeks to rally support, Crowley looked to assemble a coalition of moderates along with Black voters, a demographic that left-wing candidates have often struggled to win over in primaries.
“When people try to call me the establishment, I look at that as a slur, particularly as an African American candidate,” Crowley said ahead of the primary. “I have never run for office to protect the establishment. I’ve always been here to protect people.”
Hong’s campaign split the left
Even as Hong rocketed to frontrunner status, cracks began to show. Unlike Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, whose campaign became a massive rallying point for progressive leaders around the country, the lesser-known Hong was greeted with somewhat less enthusiasm on the left.
Most notably, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), a frequent booster of left-wing insurgent campaigns, did not endorse her, saying he was not focused on the race.
Some of that may have had to do with electability concerns, a sensitive issue for the Sanders-led movement as it looks to prove it can win in swing states this cycle, something that has eluded them since 2016.
As Hong rose in the polls, she gave a series of interviews to national media outlets where she faced questions about old rhetoric, like a call to “cancel Thanksgiving,” and some past controversial positions, like abolishing prisons and defunding the police. While she eventually made clear she would not pursue either idea in office, her sometimes disjointed answers worried allies on the left, who publicly urged her to refocus her campaign on more friendly topics.
The divide over Hong ended up sparking a broader national discussion among progressives about how — and whether — to move past the more strident language and policies around social justice issues that hit their peak during the pandemic.
“I have a local city councilman who has this saying,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) said on ABC News on Sunday. “Woke 1 was crazy.”
The debate clearly resonated with voters in Wisconsin, who were looking to their nominee to be a bulwark against a Republican nominee who had sided with Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Democrats have proven willing to break with tradition and embrace new arguments about what makes a candidate electable in 2026, but Hong wasn’t able to convince them she was worth the bet.

sources.news_title: Establishment-Backed David Crowley Pulls Off Wisconsin Upset
sources.text:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated state Assembly Member Francesca Hong in a massive upset to win the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin on Tuesday night, a victory for the state party establishment, which feared Hong’s socialist views would make her a weak candidate in the general election.
Crowley’s narrow win came despite Hong’s commanding lead in recent polling, which prompted a ferocious push by the state party establishment to consolidate behind Crowley and defeat her. It ended a topsy-turvy primary that included two leading candidates dropping out amid scandal and the resurrection of Crowley’s campaign after he initially quit in July.
On Wednesday morning, he led Hong by just 3,700 votes, equal to half of a percentage point. Both were just under 40% of the vote, with a number of other candidates ― including some who dropped out of the contest weeks ago ― splitting the remaining one-fifth.
Crowley, in his first appearance after his victory, downplayed the ideological splits within the Democratic Party and suggested voters would unite to defeat his opponent, GOP Rep. Tom Tiffany. Tiffany, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, won the Republican primary on Tuesday with the backing of President Donald Trump.
“Every one of us has something much bigger to unite around,” Crowley told reporters in Wisconsin. “And that is keeping MAGA extremism from bringing the chaos we see in Washington into our neighborhoods right here in the state of Wisconsin. From the very first day I announced this campaign, I said the real threat wasn’t any of my primary opponents. The real opponent has always been Tom Tiffany. That remains true today.”
Incumbent Gov. Tony Evers (D) campaigned relentlessly with Crowley in recent days, warning that Hong’s voluminous social media archive of controversial statements would make her a weak general election candidate, including her now-famous proclamation about hating Thanksgiving and past support for defunding the police.
“I am so proud of David — he’s the future of our Party, and I can’t wait for him to be our next governor,” Evers wrote in a 3 a.m. social media post. “For now, we polka. Tomorrow, we’re back at work to win.”
Crowley’s victory shows Democratic voters are still sensitive to warnings about electability even as their frustration with party leaders has empowered a series of major progressive victories this primary season.
Republicans clearly preferred to face Hong in the general election. The Republican Governors’ Association spent $3.6 million on ads “attacking” Hong that seemed designed to highlight left-leaning positions popular among Democratic primary voters, and Tiffany responded to Crowley’s victory with a statement comparing him to the woman he defeated.
“I’ve said all along that there’s not a dime’s worth of difference between these Democrat candidates, and David Crowley proved my point when he admitted there aren’t many policy differences between him and a socialist,” Tiffany said.
Crowley performed strongly in rural areas and in the majority-Black neighborhoods on the north side of Milwaukee. Hong did the same in college towns and in Milwaukee’s white neighborhoods. But she failed to develop a huge lead in her home county of Dane, the location of Madison and the University of Wisconsin — winning it just 44% to 36.7%, far short of the enormous margins expected of her.
While Crowley was considered the establishment candidate in the race, he bristled at the label. Considered a relatively progressive executive, Crowley came from humble origins: his parents battled drug addiction, his family was evicted three times before he was 18, and he initially dropped out of college, only to earn his degree in 2024 while serving as county executive.
“The frustration for me is because I have worked my entire life not to be labeled, not to be placed in a box,” he said in an interview last week on “Pod Save America.” “I didn’t get into this race to protect the establishment. I got into this race to protect the people, to let folks know that they deserve to have a seat at the table.”
Crowley campaigned on using an existing state budget surplus to fund education without raising local property taxes, expand child care offerings and to support rural hospitals in danger of closure.
Crowley has, however, declined to back Hong’s call for a moratorium on data center construction, an issue which powered her rise and helped draw in even GOP voters who oppose the projects. He has said he supports a “Beyonce” approach to data center construction, using the famous singer’s name as an acronym for “Bring Your Own New Clean Energy.”
Democrats, who were locked out of power by gerrymandered maps in 2011 following GOP Gov. Scott Walker’s victory, have spent 15 years trying to regain it. Holding the governor’s office and picking up a handful of seats in both the state Assembly and state Senate would give them a trifecta for the first time in a decade.
A Crowley victory in November would make him Wisconsin’s first Black governor and just the fourth Black person elected governor anywhere in the United States.

sources.news_title: Crowley Upsets Hong in Wisconsin, Graham Leads SC Senate
sources.text:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley pulled off a dramatic upset in Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor Tuesday, defeating democratic socialist state Assemblymember Francesca Hong in a race that had shown her leading by as much as 20 to 30 percentage points in the campaign's final weeks. The Associated Press called the race for Crowley around 2:34 a.m. Wednesday after a count that ran late into the night. Crowley will face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump and won his own primary comfortably, in a November race to succeed retiring Gov. Tony Evers. If elected, Crowley would become Wisconsin's first Black governor.
Crowley's win capped an unusually turbulent campaign. He briefly suspended his bid in July to back Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, then re-entered the race days later after Rodriguez withdrew amid a campaign finance controversy, picking up Evers' endorsement in the process. Hong, who had built a coalition with backing from the Madison and Milwaukee chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America, faced late scrutiny over past social media posts and questions about her viability in a state Trump carried in both 2016 and 2024. Her defeat marks a reversal from a string of progressive primary wins earlier this year in Michigan, New York and Colorado, and Democratic strategists described it as evidence that primary voters in swing states are still weighing electability heavily against ideology.
In Minnesota, Sen. Amy Klobuchar won the Democratic nomination for governor by an overwhelming margin over six lesser-known challengers, setting up a run against Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who defeated MyPillow founder Mike Lindell and health care executive Kendall Qualls for the GOP nod. Klobuchar is seeking to succeed Gov. Tim Walz, who announced earlier this year he would not seek a third term amid scrutiny over fraud allegations at state-licensed day care centers. In the state's open U.S. Senate race, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan defeated Rep. Angie Craig for the Democratic nomination in a contest that, like Wisconsin's, was cast as a proxy fight over the party's direction after 2024. Flanagan will face former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, who won the Republican Senate primary over ex-NBA player Royce White, in the race to succeed retiring Sen. Tina Smith.
South Carolina held a special Republican primary to fill the Senate seat left vacant by the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died last month at age 71. His sister, Darline Graham, whom Gov. Henry McMaster appointed to the seat just three days after her brother's death, led a field of 10 candidates with about 33 percent of the vote, according to the Associated Press. Rep. Ralph Norman finished second with roughly 25 percent, edging out Rep. Russell Fry and former Gov. Mark Sanford. Because no candidate cleared 50 percent, Graham and Norman will meet in a runoff on Aug. 25, with the winner facing Democrat Annie Andrews in November. Trump has endorsed Graham and told reporters Tuesday night he plans to campaign for her, while Norman, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, said he intends to contrast his congressional record against her lack of elected experience.
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont turned back a primary challenge from progressive state Rep. Josh Elliott by a roughly 2-to-1 margin, in what was the first primary faced by a sitting Connecticut governor in 48 years. Lamont, seeking a third term, will face Republican state Sen. Ryan Fazio in November; Republicans have not held the governor's office in Connecticut since 2011. Elliott conceded shortly before 9 p.m. and called on Democrats to unite behind Lamont for the general election. Voters in Alabama and Vermont also went to the polls Tuesday, with Alabama holding special congressional primaries tied to a new court-approved district map and Vermont selecting nominees for governor, lieutenant governor and its at-large U.S. House seat.
Taken together, Tuesday's results offered a mixed verdict for Democrats' ongoing debate over how sharply to move left ahead of the midterms. Crowley's win in Wisconsin and Lamont's comfortable defense of his seat in Connecticut favored more moderate, establishment-aligned candidates, while Flanagan's victory in Minnesota's Senate primary extended a run of success for the party's more progressive wing. Republicans, meanwhile, notched a clean sweep in their gubernatorial and Senate primaries across Wisconsin, Minnesota and South Carolina, with Trump-endorsed candidates advancing in each contest except the South Carolina Senate race, where Norman also secured a spot in the runoff without the president's backing.
The primaries unfolded against a broader backdrop of concern about the integrity of this fall's elections. In an interview released Tuesday, Trump declined to rule out declaring a national security emergency as a way to assert greater federal control over the November midterms, after a conservative media host raised the idea as an alternative to stalled legislation in the Senate. "Let me just say stranger things have happened," Trump said, adding, "I'll leave it at that." The remark followed a White House address last month on election security and earlier comments in which Trump urged Republicans to "nationalize the voting" in certain states. Legal experts have said the Constitution gives states primary authority over running elections and are divided on whether any emergency declaration invoking national security could withstand a court challenge.
With Tuesday's contests settled, attention shifts to South Carolina's Aug. 25 runoff, which will determine the Republican nominee for a seat Graham has held for less than a month, and to how the newly set matchups in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Connecticut shape spending and momentum heading into the fall. National Democratic and Republican committees are expected to make early investment decisions in the Wisconsin and Minnesota governor's races in particular, given their status as premier tests of each party's midterm strategy in swing states Trump narrowly carried in 2024.

sources.news_title: Shock Loss For DSA Candidate Hong in Wisconsin Dem Governor’s Primary
sources.text:
Shock Loss For DSA Candidate Hong in Wisconsin Dem Governor’s Primary
This race offered another reminder that voters — not pollsters, pundits, or prediction markets — ultimately decide elections.
In what is surely one of the most astounding polling misses of the 2026 primary season, Wisconsin Assembly member Francesca Hong’s commanding 20-point lead over Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in the state’s Democratic gubernatorial primary collapsed entirely once the voters weighed in.
Shortly before 4 a.m. E.T. Wednesday, The Associated Press called the race for Crowley. At that point, with more than 95% of the vote counted, he led Hong by 3,279 votes out of nearly 789,000 ballots cast. The New York Times had Crowley at 39.78%, Hong at 39.37%, and state Sen. Kelda Roys at 7.49%.
WASHINGTON (AP) — David Crowley wins Democratic nomination for governor in Wisconsin. #APRaceCall at 3:34 a.m. EDT. https://t.co/TS3eIpQI5W
— AP Race Calls (@AP_RaceCalls) August 12, 2026
Few races this primary season have seen as many twists and turns as this one.
In early July, Crowley, seeing no path to victory, suspended his campaign and endorsed Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez.
Rodriguez withdrew from the race on July 17 after her campaign was rocked by serious financial reporting problems. It was revealed that the campaign had hundreds of thousands of dollars less cash on hand than previously believed.
One day later, after securing the endorsement of Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, Crowley reentered the race.
According to The Associated Press, Evers had initially declined to endorse a candidate in the primary. His subsequent decision to throw his support behind Crowley likely reflected growing concern among the Democratic establishment that the uber progressive Hong could win the party’s nomination only to lose the general election.
Crowley and Evers have since barnstormed the state together, and clearly, their efforts have paid off.
The early frontrunner, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, suspended his campaign on July 30, the day that The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel revealed “it was investigating allegations that Barnes had leveraged his role within the state Democratic party to have sexual encounters with young women.”
The far-left Hong watched what had been a narrow lead in early July balloon to roughly 20 points by the end of the month. Her dramatic surge in the polls brought intense scrutiny to her campaign, her past, and some of her more extreme positions.
Hong, a member of the legislature’s Socialist Caucus, has spent the past few weeks trying to distance herself from some of her most radical views. But digital footprints are stubborn things.
Additionally, over the weekend, X user @SwannMarcus89 alleged that big spending by Republican political action committees may have been at least partially responsible for Hong’s spike in the polls throughout the month of July. Swann explains how he arrived at that conclusion in the post below.
So I discovered something interesting today.
I keep hearing Francesca Hong is running some innovative campaign where she isn’t spending money on TV and it’s working like a charm. This confused me because I have family in Wisconsin and I know for a fact there are tons of…
— Swann Marcus (@SwannMarcus89) August 8, 2026
Crowley’s victory complicates matters for Republican gubernatorial nominee Tom Tiffany. Hong was widely viewed as the easier opponent to beat. In a purple state like Wisconsin, her radical worldview was expected to be a tough sell among independent voters and even some Democrats.
Ahead of the primary, the RealClearPolitics polling average of head-to-head matchups with Hong showed Tiffany leading by 1.7 points. Against Crowley, however, Tiffany trailed by 2 points.
The shift becomes even more apparent when looking at Polymarket’s odds on which party is likely to win the governorship in November. On Monday, when Hong was still widely expected to capture the Democratic nomination, Republicans were given a 59.5% chance of winning the general election, compared with 41.5% for Democrats.
By early Wednesday morning, the picture had completely changed. With Crowley emerging as the Democratic nominee, the odds had swung sharply in the opposite direction: Democrats’ chances had surged to 69.5%, while Republicans’ had plunged to just 29%.
[Note: Polymarket odds can be viewed by scrolling down on the RCP page for this race.]
Crowley’s victory is a remarkable political resurrection and great news for Wisconsin Democrats. Just one month ago, Crowley saw so little hope of winning the nomination that he dropped out of the race. He returned only after Rodriguez’s campaign imploded. With a hearty endorsement from the governor, he proceeded to defeat a candidate who, according to the polls, had opened up a seemingly insurmountable lead.
For Republicans, however, Hong’s defeat changes the complexion of the general election considerably. Tiffany will no longer face a socialist opponent carrying a long record of controversial positions in a closely divided state. Instead, he will face Crowley, a more conventional Democrat who has already demonstrated an ability to defy expectations. The battle for Wisconsin’s governorship just became a very different race.
This race offered another reminder that voters — not pollsters, pundits, or prediction markets — ultimately decide elections.

sources.news_title: Socialist speed bump in Wisconsin, but left sweeps other key races
sources.text:
Socialist speed bump in Wisconsin, but left sweeps other key races
So far, the left of the party won three of the four contests, with the notable exception of Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, who fell short against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley
(AP Photo/Kayla Wolf)
In Tuesday’s newsletter, we wrote that four major Democratic primary races — in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Connecticut — would be key tests of the depth of the anti-establishment, anti-Israel left’s staying power.
So far, the left of the party won three of the four contests, with the notable exception of Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, who fell short against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley — in the night’s most high-profile race testing whether a socialist can win the Democratic nomination for an executive role in a pivotal battleground state.
Hong, who drew criticism from leading Democrats over her record of comments attacking Thanksgiving, support for defunding the police and overall embrace of the DSA’s radical platform, underperformed the primary polls showing her with a substantial lead in the race. But as Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers and leading Democratic officials warned that her nomination could cost Democrats the governorship, her lead dissipated amid concerns about her electability come November.
Of note: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), the two leading members of the ideological left in Congress, declined to endorse Hong’s campaign.
The establishment’s unified — and effective — show of force against Hong offered a stark contrast to party leaders’ efforts in Michigan to stop far-left candidate Abdul El-Sayed from winning the nomination. In that race, party leaders were more equivocal in their support of Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI), with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) declining to support Stevens’ candidacy despite their similar political backgrounds. Even Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who offered a late endorsement to Stevens, didn’t go after El-Sayed’s electability like Evers has in his comments speaking out against Hong.
The socialist speed bump in Wisconsin, however, was seemingly the only exception to an overall dominant showing from progressive candidates, highlighted by the left’s successes in Minnesota.
In the pivotal Minnesota Senate race, progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan comfortably outdistanced moderate Rep. Angie Craig (D-MN) by nearly 20 points. Flanagan is one of Minnesota’s most progressive statewide officials, and campaigned as a strident critic of Israel. Flanagan will be facing former NBC Sports sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, who easily won the Republican nomination. Republican leaders believe Tafoya has broad appeal given her national television work, but winning a blue state like Minnesota given the GOP headwinds will be a very difficult task — even against a less-electable challenger like Flanagan.
The left is also celebrating the results in Craig’s suburban Minneapolis district, where the most anti-Israel and furthest-left candidate, former state Sen. Matt Little, easily outpaced two more-moderate challengers, including pro-Israel state Sen. Matt Klein. Little will be facing GOP state Sen. Eric Pratt in the general election, and will be favored in a district that Kamala Harris carried by six points in 2024.
In Connecticut, Rep. John Larson (D-CT) was handily defeated by a younger political challenger in former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, who moved to Larson’s left on Israel during the campaign, but was broadly seen as the more future-oriented candidate. The seat, with the largest Jewish constituency in the Nutmeg State, is a safe Democratic district.
On the Republican side, Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) will be squaring off against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) in a special election runoff later this month to fill the full term of her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat. Graham won 33% of the Republican vote in the crowded race, while Norman won 25%. Norman outpaced Rep. Russell Fry (R-SC) — the other sitting member of Congress in the race — by five points.
Norman is a hard-line fiscal conservative who was one of former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy’s (R-CA) biggest antagonists in his battle to remain as House leader. He also endorsed Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential campaign, a factor that could lead President Donald Trump to redouble his backing for Graham’s candidacy.

sources.news_title: David Crowley’s Chances of Beating Tom Tiffany After Wisconsin Primary Win
sources.text:
Democrats' chances of holding on to the Wisconsin governor's office have surged on prediction markets after moderate Democrat David Crowley won his party's gubernatorial primary over progressive state Representative Francesca Hong.
Crowley, who is seeking to become Wisconsin's first Black governor, narrowly defeated Hong after pitching himself as the candidate best positioned to defeat U.S. Representative Tom Tiffany, who received President Donald Trump's endorsement and won the Republican primary, in November.
Crowley, who had quit the race in early July, revived his campaign with the endorsement of outgoing Democratic Governor Tony Evers less than two weeks later. Newsweek has contacted the Crowley and Tiffany campaigns for comment via email.
On prediction markets, Republican odds of flipping the governorship in November had surged above Democrats' in the days leading up to Tuesday's primary, as Hong appeared set to become the nominee. Public polls had shown her with a commanding lead over Crowley and other candidates.
However, the Associated Press called the race for Crowley early Wednesday morning after Hong conceded, and prediction markets once again favor Democrats to win the gubernatorial election in November.
As of 8 a.m. Eastern time, Kashi has given Democrats a 78 percent chance of holding on to the governor's office this fall, up from 39.4 percent on Sunday. Republicans' odds have fallen to 22 percent on the prediction market, from 61.8 percent on Sunday.
Democrats' odds of winning in November have also climbed on rival prediction market Polymarket. As of 5:30 a.m., it gives Democrats a 77 percent chance of winning in November, up from 41 percent a day ago. Republican odds have fallen to 22 percent, down from 51 percent on Monday.
Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future.
The Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball both rank the Wisconsin gubernatorial race as a toss-up.
Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Newsweek on Wednesday that Crowley's win "likely boosts Democrats' chances to win the governor's race against the GOP's Tiffany in Wisconsin."
"His nomination erases electability concerns about how Hong's more ideologically extreme agenda would play in the general election," he continued.
Still, Panagopoulos added: "Democrats might be temporarily breathing a sigh of relief; however, they will still likely have a dogfight on their hands heading into November."
Both Candidates Must Win Over Independents
To emerge victorious in November, Crowley and Tiffany will have to win over the moderate and independent voters who are critical in the swing state known for razor-thin election margins.
Crowley "is focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results," Garren Randolph, his campaign manager, said in a statement after the race was called.
Tiffany appealed to those voters in his victory speech on Tuesday night.
"Whatever your political label—Republican, independent, politically homeless, or Democrat, there's a place for you in the commonsense movement," he said.
"If you want your children and grandchildren to grow up in a land of opportunity, join us," he added.
Mainstream Democrats Rallied Behind Crowley
Crowley's victory comes after he secured the backing of more mainstream Democrats, who fear candidates from the party's left flank will struggle to beat Republicans in November.
Some establishment Democrats worried that Hong and her platform would be a tougher sell among moderate and independent voters.
Jim Kessler, the executive vice president for policy at the centrist group Third Way, said the skepticism reflected a structural reality of governor's races rather than bias against Hong specifically.
"Voters are a lot more forgiving in legislative races than in governor's races when it comes to ideology," Kessler told Newsweek. In a governor's race, he said, "the officeholder is one of one," and voters weigh what a candidate means "for their taxes, their business, their schools and their safety."
While Hong had energized left-wing voters, prominent national progressives—including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders—did not endorse her despite supporting other prominent progressive candidates, such as Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
"My focus has been in winning back the Congress, winning back the House, and positioning ourselves to have the best chance possible to win the Senate," Ocasio-Cortez said on ABC's This Week on Sunday when asked why she hadn't endorsed Hong.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Shakeema Edwards.

sources.news_title: Is the Progressive March on Hold?
sources.text:
A slate of midterm primaries yesterday, August 11, exposed a number of truisms, but also fault lines, in the apparently inexorable progressive march to reshape the Democratic Party. While plenty of races went to the insurgent socialist wing, not everything was plain sailing, with the Democratic Socialist candidate for the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, Francesca Hong, falling at the last hurdle. The results hint at more than just a question of enthusiasm.
Talk of free stuff for everyone is, naturally, quite the draw when it comes to building excitement around a candidate. And although such ephemeral promises make for good soundbites, canny voters appear unwilling - in some cases - to jettison the electability factor.
A Socialist Fail in Wisconsin
An incredibly close primary contest in Wisconsin to replace outgoing incumbent Governor Tony Evers ended with a victory for the “moderate” Democrat David Crowley, who narrowly beat progressive Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidate Hong. With a final tally of 39.8% to 39.4% (a difference of just several thousand votes), her loss is a rare blip that could signal an element of political sanity when it comes to winning in November.
Hong has been the focus of innumerable column inches in recent weeks, not only for her fairly typical DSA stances, but also for her comments regarding her hatred of Thanksgiving. It is these types of remarks that spook the generally moderate primary voters. They may well agree with her assessment of America’s most unique holiday, but understanding that it will alienate the all-important independent voters come November could explain why the polling got it so wrong.
As The New York Times reported just yesterday:
“In all, nine polls were fielded in the three months before the election, but only two have come out since the candidate field settled — and one of those was an internal poll for Mr. Crowley. Even that internal poll showed him well behind Ms. Hong.”
In fact, of the five major polls conducted since July, Ms. Hong’s worst result was plus 11 points over Crowley, and her average lead was almost 17 points. Heading into the primary election, she must have been extremely confident.
Electability Matters
Up and down the country, we have seen progressive insurgents win big races – and yet these have almost entirely been in deep blue areas. Wisconsin is a swing state by any definition, and while voters in places like Maryland and California can comfortably choose any candidate that takes their fancy knowing that a Democrat will win regardless, the Badger State electorate enjoys no such luxury.
Most estimates put Republicans and Democrats at roughly 30% each of the national vote share, with independents making up the remaining 40%. These crucial voters decide elections. It seems unlikely that many would have opted for a candidate who openly trashed Thanksgiving, only to later claim her adoration of cranberries in a politically expedient 180.
Democrat primary voters, it appears, determined that winning a primary contest is less important than winning the actual election. Their heart-of-heart hopes were with Hong (as the polling demonstrates), but political reality bites extremely hard. Choosing between a “moderate” Democrat and a Republican of any stripe in the governor’s mansion was perhaps not so tough a call for the party faithful.
A Democrat Problem With No Good Answers
As the Associated Press wrote, “Hong’s loss in Wisconsin may have doused the momentum, but it’s far from snuffing it out. A democratic socialist coming close to victory in a battleground state sends a clear message: There’s unignorable angst among the party’s voters.” A valid assessment, but one that ignores the political volatility unfolding within the ranks.
Blue states are safe havens for the establishment wing of the party; swing states are – as their name suggests – volatile in terms of reliability. If the core party has to fight on two fronts (GOP battles and progressive battles), maintaining any amount of electoral success long-term becomes a costly conundrum.
As progressives gain power and prominence in the safe-haven seats, the Old Guard may find itself relegated to tight matches in swing states, fighting for its very existence.
